name: metapool
workload: Construction and reserve() of mtp::vault (pool-backed dynamic array) vs std::vector (std::allocator/ptmalloc) and std::pmr::vector (pmr pool + monotonic_buffer_resource), across element counts.
claimed_speedup: README headline: up to 1300x faster construction and reserve() than std::vector and up to 3.5x faster than std::pmr::vector. Results image: reserve microbenchmark 939.81x-1380.19x faster than std::vector (one outlier of 4762.93x at large2) and 2.65x-3.63x faster than pmr::vector; emplace 1.20x-1.61x faster than std; selective construct path 1.21x-15.40x faster than std; churn simulation ranges from 1.58x slower to 1.66x faster than std; raw alloc 1.81x-287.40x faster than malloc.
compiler_and_flags: clang 20.1.8; -O3 -march=native -fstrict-aliasing -flto
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8840U, Arch Linux kernel 6.15.8, glibc 2.42 (ptmalloc), 64GB DDR5
tradeoffs: Compile-time fixed pool layout (metaset) must be tuned per workload; no general fallback beyond configured strides; header-only but requires C++23; cannot grow arbitrarily beyond the preallocated arena without a reset.
caveats: The ~1000x+ figures come only from the reserve microbenchmark, where each frame creates one std::vector, calls reserve(count), and frees it. glibc malloc/free of large blocks likely dominates that path, so it is not general alloc/free churn. In the more realistic tables the gains shrink to 1.2x-1.6x (emplace), and churn simulation is 1.06x-1.58x slower than std for 4096B and 16384B elements. Results are published only as a PNG image. New project (created Aug 2025, 37 stars) with no independent verification found.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'C++ pool allocator faster than std::allocator benchmark github'

verification.tier_reason: Benchmark code is public in benchmark/ (benchmark_micro.hpp, benchmark_selective.hpp, CMakeLists.txt, build.sh), and the README states clang 20.1.8, -O3 -march=native -fstrict-aliasing -flto, and an AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8840U. It compares directly against std::vector with std::allocator and against std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource. Flags are stated, so the >50x cap does not apply.
verification.notes: Headline numbers match the README text and the results image. baseline_stdlib = libstdc++ is inferred: build.sh adds -stdlib=libc++ only on macOS, and the test system is Arch Linux clang, which defaults to libstdc++. Per-case numbers were read from the results PNG (https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c7692e54-...).

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: up to ~1300x faster construction/reserve than std::vector (std::allocator); up to ~3.5x faster than std::pmr::vector (pool resource)
corrected_fields.caveats: The ~1300x figure comes from a narrow construction+reserve microbenchmark (bypassing malloc/realloc growth entirely), not sustained alloc/free churn; the ~3.5x-vs-pmr figure is more representative of general use. New project (created Aug 2025), 37 stars, no independent third-party verification found.

name: NUMAlloc
workload: PARSEC (native inputs), five CORAL-2 OpenMP/MPI apps (Nekbone, QMCPACK, LAMMPS, AMG, Quicksilver) and real apps (Apache httpd, MySQL, Memcached, SQLite, Aget, Pfscan, Pbzip2) at 128 threads on an 8-node NUMA machine, plus Hoard synthetic scalability tests (threadtest, larson, cache-scratch, cache-thrash)
claimed_speedup: 15.7% faster on average than the second-best allocator (mimalloc-1.6.7) and 20.9% faster than the default Linux allocator (glibc 2.28) across PARSEC, CORAL-2 OpenMP/MPI and real applications. 26.1% faster than glibc on the OpenMP/MPI apps alone. Best case fluidanimate: up to 5.3x faster than glibc, 4.8x faster than TBB and 4.6x faster than mimalloc (ISMM'23 manuscript). The earlier SC'22 draft (SC2022/evaluation.tex) reported 19.0% vs glibc, 6.8x vs Scalloc, and a Rodinia average of 2.44x vs glibc / 2.33x vs mimalloc. The Rodinia claim is commented out of the ISMM'23 manuscript.
compiler_and_flags: GCC-8.3.0 on Linux Debian 10. The paper gives no optimization flags; the repo's source/Makefile builds the allocator with -g -O2 -std=c++14. Hyperthreading off, transparent huge pages and AutoNUMA enabled, 128 threads (= core count).
hardware: Intel Xeon(R) Platinum 8153, 2.00GHz, 8 NUMA nodes x 16 physical cores (128 cores total), 512GB RAM, 32KB L1/1MB L2 per core, 22MB LLC per node
tradeoffs: About 10-12% higher memory footprint than the default allocator due to transparent-huge-page use (drops to comparable with THP disabled); designed around NUMA-aware node/thread binding, so benefits are largest on multi-socket/multi-node machines and smaller on single-socket systems; needs origin-aware object return and an interleaved heap that can hurt serial-phase-heavy applications.
caveats: No top-level LICENSE. Some source files (e.g. libnumalloc.cpp, inherited from FreeGuard) carry GPL-2.0-or-later headers, but most NUMA-specific files (pernodeheap, perthreadheap, interheap) have no license header, so the license is unclear (usability=reference). The repo bundles sources and paper drafts for about 10 UTSASRG projects plus many source-* variant folders, and source/Makefile is configured for NUMA_NODES=2, so which build produced the paper numbers is not obvious. The original benchmark_url was an unpublished SC'22 draft whose numbers differ from the later ISMM'23 manuscript (19.0% vs 20.9% over glibc; Rodinia claim dropped). The draft also contradicts itself on fluidanimate (5.3x vs 2.9x over glibc). Last push 2023-03-01 (>3 years ago): abandoned.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch 'memory allocator faster than std::allocator malloc evaluation paper' -> gh search repos "numalloc" -> UTSASRG/numalloc SC2022/evaluation.tex, abstract.tex, intro.tex

verification.tier_reason: The allocator source is public (source/) and GCC-8.3.0 plus the Xeon Platinum 8153 CPU are stated. But no optimization flags are given for the benchmarks, and the PARSEC/CORAL-2/Rodinia harness is not in the repo, so it is not A. The work was published peer-reviewed at ISMM 2023 (DOI 10.1145/3591195.3595276, confirmed via Crossref), so it is B.
verification.notes: The numbers in the original record do appear verbatim in SC2022/evaluation.tex, but that is a pre-publication draft. The peer-reviewed venue is ISMM 2023, so benchmark_url and claimed_speedup were re-pointed to the ISMM2023 manuscript in the repo; the published ACM text itself was not opened. Downgraded from A to B because the paper states no compile flags and the repo has no benchmark harness.

corrected_fields.workload: PARSEC + Rodinia OpenMP/MPI multithreaded applications and Hoard-suite microbenchmarks (threadtest, larson, false-sharing) run with up to 128 threads across an 8-node NUMA machine

name: SuperMalloc
baseline: best of DLmalloc, JEmalloc, Hoard, and TBBmalloc
workload: malloc-test multithreaded allocate/free microbenchmark at 1, 8 (with hardware transactional memory), and 32 threads on 64-bit Linux
claimed_speedup: ~2.1x faster than the best of DLmalloc/JEmalloc/Hoard/TBBmalloc with 1 thread; 2.75x faster with 8 threads + HTM; 3.4x faster with 32 threads (no HTM)
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.8.3 on Linux 3.15.7 / glibc 2.18 (Fedora 20), per the paper. Release build flags -O3 -flto -pthread -fPIC, plus -mrtm for the HTM build (release/Makefile, Makefile.include). Compared against Hoard 3.10, jemalloc 3.6.0, tbb43_20140724 and DLmalloc 2.8.6.
hardware: Intel Core i7-4770 (Haswell-DT, 4 cores / 8 HW threads, 3.4GHz, 1 socket) for the HTM results; 2-socket 16-core Intel Xeon E5-2665 (Sandy Bridge, 2.4GHz, 32 HW threads) for the non-HTM 32-thread results
tradeoffs: Full-speed path requires Haswell+ hardware transactional memory; ships a separate pthread-lock build (libsupermalloc_pthread.so) for machines without HTM. Uses more virtual address space via a superblock design. Author Bradley Kuszmaul's ISMM'15 paper implementation, not a maintained production allocator.
caveats: The benchmark toolchain (gcc 4.8.3 / glibc 2.18 / Fedora 20) is from 2015. The last commit on any branch is 2017-10-25 (GitHub pushed_at of 2019-11-15 has no matching commit), and there is no recent head-to-head vs mimalloc/snmalloc/rpmalloc. The numbers come from the author's own malloc-test variant in the ISMM'15 paper. The paper's 'DLmalloc' is standalone Doug Lea dlmalloc 2.8.6 linked separately, not glibc's ptmalloc2-based default malloc, so glibc malloc itself was not measured. The fastest path relies on Haswell TSX/HTM; a pthread-mutex build also exists. Dual-licensed: MIT (expat) or GPLv3-or-later.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch '"SuperMalloc" OR "scalloc" OR "Mesh allocator" benchmark faster than jemalloc tcmalloc paper' -> gh search repos "supermalloc" -> repo paper/ismm15/supermalloc.tex

verification.tier_reason: The ISMM'15 paper source states gcc 4.8.3 / glibc 2.18 / Fedora 20 and the CPUs (i7-4770, Xeon E5-2665). The benchmark code is public in the same repo (tests/new-malloc-test.c, with raw data in paper/ismm15/*.data), and release/Makefile sets -O3 -flto (-mrtm for HTM). That meets A.
verification.notes: The abstract states 2.1x / 2.75x / 3.4x over the best of DLmalloc/JEmalloc/Hoard/TBBmalloc verbatim. Metadata fixes: the license is MIT OR GPL-3.0-or-later (the GPL text says 'or any later version'), and last_commit is 2017-10-25, not 2019-11-15. compared_against_cpp_std_directly is set to false because the 'DLmalloc' baseline is standalone dlmalloc 2.8.6, not the system glibc malloc.

corrected_fields.hardware: 4-core i7-4770 (Haswell-DT, 3.4GHz, 1 socket + hyperthreading) for the HTM results; 16-core 2-socket 2.4GHz Xeon-class machine for the larger-thread-count results
corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.8.3 on Linux 3.15.7 / glibc 2.18 (Fedora 20); also uses Haswell hardware transactional memory (HTM) intrinsics for the lock-elision fast path
corrected_fields.caveats: Benchmark toolchain (gcc 4.8.3 / glibc 2.18 / Fedora 20) is from 2015; repo has had no commits since 2019-11-15 so there is no recent head-to-head vs jemalloc/mimalloc/snmalloc/rpmalloc. Numbers come from the project's own malloc-test benchmark (bundled in the same repo as the paper source), not an independent third party, but compiler, flags-equivalent build config, and exact CPU models are all stated in the paper text, so it meets tier A.

name: Hoard
baseline: Solaris default allocator, Ptmalloc (glibc malloc backing operator new/delete)
workload: Uniprocessor and multiprocessor (1-14 way Sun Enterprise 5000) allocation-intensive benchmarks: threadtest, shbench, Larson server simulation, active/passive false-sharing tests, BEMengine PDE solver, Barnes-Hut n-body solver, plus single-threaded espresso/Ghostscript/LRUsim/p2c.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract: up to 60x over the standard Solaris allocator on 14 processors, and up to 18x over the next best allocator tested. At 14 processors: Larson 18x faster than Ptmalloc, threadtest 278% faster than Ptmalloc, shbench 85% faster than Ptmalloc. Uniprocessor: BEMengine 10.3% faster than the Solaris allocator, but the average over the uniprocessor benchmarks is 6.2% slower than Solaris.
compiler_and_flags: GNU C++ at -O6 (Sun Workshop C++ compiler 5.0 used only for Barnes-Hut)
hardware: Sun Enterprise 5000, 2GB RAM, 14x 400MHz UltraSPARC CPUs, 4MB L2 cache, Solaris 7
stars_or_usage: 1.25k stars; historically used by AOL, Cisco, SAP, Reuters, RBC and others per README; standard allocator option in SPEC CPU2006
tradeoffs: Multi-heap design trades some memory for scalability (bounded blowup, not zero); link-time/LD_PRELOAD drop-in malloc replacement, not a std::allocator template adapter; per-processor heap hashing can cause heap/thread collisions.
caveats: Primary evidence is the ASPLOS 2000 paper, run on 14x 400MHz UltraSPARC with Solaris 7 against the Solaris and Ptmalloc allocators of that era; the GNU C++ version is unstated. Uniprocessor, Hoard averaged 6.2% slower than the Solaris allocator (shbench +49.2%, espresso +15.9%, Ghostscript +10.6% runtime). The current README adds first-party modern results (code in benchmarks/, 192-core 2-node AMD EPYC, exact CPU model, compiler, and flags unstated, charts only). Those results claim 1.3-1.5x higher Larson throughput than glibc, mimalloc, and jemalloc, and 1.6x faster than glibc at 128 threads on NUMA. The README concedes that jemalloc wins linux-scalability. Hoard is also in daanx/mimalloc-bench as 'hd', but those results are chart images only.
found_via: GitHub: found via daanx/mimalloc-bench README allocator list ('hd' = Hoard); followed citation to the ASPLOS 2000 paper

verification.tier_reason: The peer-reviewed ASPLOS 2000 paper compares Hoard against the Solaris 7 default allocator and Ptmalloc (glibc) on a 14-way Sun Enterprise 5000 with GNU C++ -O6. The compiler version is unstated and the benchmark code is not tied to the paper, so it falls short of A.
verification.notes: The old record had '10.6% faster (BEMengine)'. The paper's BEMengine figure is 10.3% faster; 10.6% is Ghostscript, where Hoard is slower. The earlier caveat said no modern reproduction exists, but the README now has modern first-party benchmarks against glibc. Those are tier C material, so the paper keeps this entry at B.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Up to 60x over the standard Solaris allocator and up to 18x over the next-best allocator (Ptmalloc) at 14 processors (paper abstract); threadtest 278% faster than Ptmalloc at 14 procs; shbench 85% faster than Ptmalloc at 14 procs; Larson 18x faster than Ptmalloc at 14 procs; BEMengine 10.6% faster than Solaris allocator uniprocessor
corrected_fields.caveats: Primary quantitative evidence is a peer-reviewed ASPLOS 2000 paper run on 26-year-old hardware (UltraSPARC/Solaris 7) against the Solaris and Ptmalloc allocators of that era, not a modern libstdc++/libc++/MSVC STL build; no current reproduction with stated modern compiler/flags/hardware was found this session, so capped at Tier B rather than A. The GitHub repo itself is actively maintained in 2026 as a drop-in malloc replacement, and Hoard is also included (as 'hd') in the independent daanx/mimalloc-bench suite, though that page's results are chart images only, not text numbers.

name: scalloc
baseline: ptmalloc2 (glibc's default malloc, part of GNU libc; extends Doug Lea's dlmalloc)
workload: SPEC CPU2006 483.xalancbmk single-threaded allocation-intensive workload, plus threadtest/shbench/larson multithreaded microbenchmarks and an ACDC-generated producer-consumer workload
claimed_speedup: About 1.28x SPEC ratio vs ptmalloc2 on single-threaded 483.xalancbmk (read from the Figure 5 bar chart, derived from page data). Here scalloc is mid-pack, below TCMalloc (~1.345), llalloc (~1.33), TBB (~1.29) and SuperMalloc (~1.285), and the paper says the differences among the best allocators are small. For multithreaded workloads the paper claims scalloc 'increases performance on average while consuming less memory than the previously fastest allocator (TBB)' and outperforms/outscales all allocators for varying object sizes that fit virtual spans.
hardware: UMA machine, 4x 10-core 2GHz Intel Xeon E7-4850 (2 hardware threads/core), 32KB L1D, 32KB L1I, 256KB L2/core, 24MB L3/processor, 128GB RAM, Linux kernel 3.8.0
tradeoffs: Reserves up to 32TB of virtual address space per arena (relies on on-demand paging / madvise to keep physical memory low); distributed via LD_PRELOAD on Linux / DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES on OSX; needs overcommit accounting and transparent-huge-pages tuned for best results.
caveats: The OOPSLA'15 paper (arXiv v2, Aug 2015) is 10+ years old. The current README says the allocator was 'completely rewritten from scratch' since the paper and says to benchmark the current version; the separate cksystemsgroup/scalloc-artifact repo was last updated 2018-03-20. Today's numbers may therefore differ from the paper's. The paper states no compiler or optimization flags. The xalancbmk values exist only as bars in Figure 5, not as printed numbers.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch '"SuperMalloc" OR "scalloc" OR "Mesh allocator" benchmark faster than jemalloc tcmalloc paper' -> gh search repos "scalloc" -> arxiv.org/pdf/1503.09006

verification.tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed OOPSLA'15 paper (Artifact Evaluated) comparing against ptmalloc2 on SPEC 483.xalancbmk and threadtest/shbench/larson/ACDC, with hardware (4x Xeon E7-4850) stated. Neither the paper nor the artifact README (only 'tested on Ubuntu 14.04') gives the compiler or flags, so it is B, not A.
verification.notes: The record's '~1.33x, on par with TCMalloc ~1.34x' misread Figure 5: the ~1.33 bar is llalloc, and scalloc's bar is about 1.28. claimed_speedup was corrected and verdict downgraded (tier stays B). The 'artifact not updated since 2019' caveat was corrected to 2018-03-20.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: ~1.33x SPEC ratio vs ptmalloc2 on single-threaded 483.xalancbmk (Figure 5, on par with TCMalloc's ~1.34x); among the fastest and most memory-efficient allocators (previously TBB was fastest) across the multithreaded threadtest/shbench/larson suite
corrected_fields.caveats: OOPSLA'15 paper (arXiv v2, Aug 2015) is now 10+ years old; the current repo README says the allocator was 'completely rewritten from scratch' since the paper and points benchmarking at a separate cksystemsgroup/scalloc-artifact repo that has not been updated since 2019, so today's numbers may differ from the paper's. Exact compiler/version and optimization flags used for the SPEC run were not found in the extracted paper text, so tier is capped at B rather than A.

name: arena-allocator (ShortAlloc)
baseline: operator new/delete (GNU/glibc malloc via std::vector's default std::allocator)
workload: std::vector<TestClass>::emplace_back of 100 objects of sizes 8B-8KB, using a stack-backed bump-pointer Arena + ShortAlloc STL allocator vs the default heap allocator, measured on QuickBench (AWS-hosted).
claimed_speedup: Stack/arena allocator 2.2x-4.4x faster for objects up to 512B, and 93x-230x faster for 1KB-8KB objects (crossing glibc's mmap threshold)
compiler_and_flags: clang 17.0, -O3, -std=c++20, libstdc++ ('gnu' lib), per the QuickBench options of the linked benchmarks (not stated in the README)
hardware: QuickBench-hosted AWS machine pool: the QuickBench result context shows 1 CPU at 2300 MHz, 32KB L1d, 256KB L2, 45MB L3; CPU model unstated. The README includes QuickBench's disclaimer that absolute timings are unreliable.
stars_or_usage: 9 stars; featured in a Hacker News 'Show HN' post
tradeoffs: Bump allocator: cannot free individual objects out of order, only the whole arena at once (or most-recent-first); backed by a fixed-size std::array, so capacity is bounded by the configured arena size; not thread-safe.
caveats: The README does not state compiler or flags, but the QuickBench runs used clang 17.0 -O3 with libstdc++. The CPU model is unknown and QuickBench's shared AWS pool makes absolute durations unreliable, so it stays at Tier C. The 93x-230x ratios for 1KB-8KB objects coincide with crossing glibc's mmap threshold (as the README explains), so they are not a general allocator speed claim. The arena cannot free non-top allocations. There is no LICENSE file, so usability is 'reference' only.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'arena allocator C++ github faster than operator new' -> Hacker News 'Show HN: C++ Arena Allocator That's 200x+ Faster Than GNU Malloc'

verification.tier_reason: First-party QuickBench numbers compare against std::vector with the default allocator (glibc malloc). The code is public (arena-benchmark.cpp and the QuickBench links), and the QuickBench options show clang 17.0 -O3 with libstdc++. The CPU model is unknown (shared AWS pool), so it cannot be A.
verification.notes: All README table numbers match (2.2x-4.4x up to 512B; 93x, 150x, 190x, 230x for 1K-8K). Compiler and flags were retrieved from the QuickBench API (quick-bench.com/quick/<id>). The Show HN post exists (2025-03-13, 2 points).

corrected_fields.hardware: QuickBench-hosted AWS machine pool; CPU model and load unstated (README includes explicit disclaimer that absolute QuickBench timings are unreliable)
corrected_fields.caveats: Compiler and optimization flags are not stated, and several ratios (93x-230x) exceed the 50x implausibility threshold, coinciding with crossing glibc's mmap allocation threshold (a known artifact of that one size range, not a general allocator speed claim) -- capped at Tier C rather than A. QuickBench's own disclaimer says absolute durations on its shared AWS pool are 'meaningless' beyond relative comparison. No LICENSE file in the repo, so usability is 'reference' only, not 'copyable'.

name: arena-allocator (yaroslavaristov)
baseline: malloc/free (system C allocator; the benchmark calls malloc/free directly, not operator new/delete)
workload: Google Benchmark: allocate N (1-1024) 64-byte objects then release them in bulk (arena reset() vs N free() calls, both inside the timed loop), plus a mixed 8/64/256-byte alloc+release batch
claimed_speedup: 10x-27x faster sequential allocation than malloc on AMD EPYC 7763 (N=1 to 1024 objects), 15x faster on a mixed-size batch; on Apple M1 (virtualized) 32x-342x faster sequential allocation and 15x on the mixed batch
compiler_and_flags: g++-14 (hard-coded via CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER in CMakeLists.txt; exact minor version not stated), C++23, Release: -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -Wall -Wextra -Werror -DNDEBUG
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (GitHub Codespaces, x86_64, native); Apple M1 (aarch64, via OrbStack virtualization -- author notes 'not native hardware')
tradeoffs: Bump-pointer only: no per-object free, just a bulk reset(); fixed power-of-two capacity decided at construction; not a general-purpose allocator (no fragmentation handling, no shrink/grow); single header, single contributor, unaudited.
caveats: Very new (last commit 2026-07-21), 1-star personal project, not peer reviewed. EPYC 7763 numbers come from a shared GitHub Codespaces VM. The largest multiples (97x-342x on Apple M1) were measured under OrbStack virtualization, which the README itself calls not native hardware; the malloc side there may be a non-glibc libc. The workload favors a bump allocator by construction: the arena releases everything with one O(1) reset while malloc pays N individual frees, and the arena has no per-object free.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: gh search repos "arena allocator" "faster than malloc"

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded from C to A. The benchmark code is public (benchmarks/bench.cpp, Google Benchmark, arena vs malloc/free), and CMakeLists.txt pins the compiler to g++-14 with Release flags -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -DNDEBUG. The README names the CPUs (AMD EPYC 7763; Apple M1 under OrbStack). The >50x cap does not apply because flags are stated.
verification.notes: All README numbers match the record (10x-27x and 15x on EPYC; 32x-342x and 15x on M1). The tier is upgraded to A because the compiler (g++-14) is pinned in CMakeLists.txt and flags plus CPU are stated. If the pipeline requires the compiler to be named on the results page itself, it drops back to C.

corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: Release build, -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -Wall -Wextra -Werror -DNDEBUG (compiler name/version not stated)
corrected_fields.workload: Sequential allocation of 1-1024 fixed-size objects and a mixed small/medium/large-object batch, arena bump-pointer vs plain malloc
corrected_fields.caveats: Very new (pushed within the last ~2 months), 1-star personal project, not peer reviewed. The largest claimed multiples (97x-342x on Apple M1) were measured on virtualized (OrbStack) hardware that the README itself calls non-native/unreliable, and exceed the 50x implausibility threshold, so tier is capped at C rather than A/B despite stated compiler flags and hardware. Comparing a no-free bump allocator against general-purpose malloc is a favorable, narrow workload (arena wins almost by construction once frees are removed from the critical path).

name: ltalloc
workload: Same multi-threaded small-object alloc/dealloc stress test used in the smmalloc benchmark table (Windows/i7-2600 and PS4), comparing ltalloc's throughput against CRT malloc.
claimed_speedup: On Windows 10/i7-2600: ~2.6x faster than crt single-threaded (62,525,965 vs 23,853,865) and ~1.9x at 5 threads (27,333,887 vs 14,636,381) (derived from page data). On PS4: ~6.4x faster than crt single-threaded (28,571,429 vs 4,444,444) and ~44x at 4 threads (14,683,637 vs 332,095) (derived from page data). Units are not stated on the page (higher is better).
hardware: Windows 10, Intel Core i7-2600; PlayStation 4
tradeoffs: Overrides global operator new/delete directly (not a std::allocator wrapper); best suited for many small (<256B) allocations; peak performance relies on LTO/inlining of the size-class computation.
caveats: The main numbers come from the third-party smmalloc README table: compiler, flags, and units are unstated, the workload is not described on the page, and the current smmalloc perf code no longer benchmarks ltalloc. On the i7-2600 table, ltalloc trails rpmalloc, hoard, and smmalloc. The earlier caveat was wrong: ltalloc's own README FAQ does have a first-party results table, published as an image. That table covers 128-byte alloc/free from concurrent threads on several Windows/Linux machines, with the default allocator 6.21x-218.75x slower than ltalloc (i7 2600/Win7 single-thread: 16.0 vs 165.0 M ops/s per thread). The linked Xeon/Debian chart (googlecode) is dead. The repo has commits in 2026 and is not GitHub-archived or a fork.
found_via: GitHub: harvested from SergeyMakeev/smmalloc README benchmark table while researching smmalloc

verification.tier_reason: The smmalloc README table compares ltalloc against crt (the default runtime malloc) on i7-2600/Windows 10 and PS4, but compiler, flags, and units are unstated. The smmalloc repo's current perf code no longer includes ltalloc. ltalloc's own README table is first-party with partial methodology. Both are C.
verification.notes: Numbers match the smmalloc table, but the record's ratios were not marked as derived, so they are now tagged. benchmark_url is left as smmalloc (text table). The ltalloc README table (https://i.imgur.com/fiR9C9M.png) is an alternative first-party source with larger ratios, but its flags are unstated and some ratios are >50x.

name: Boost.Fiber
workload: skynet microbenchmark (ported from atemerev/skynet): spawn 10 threads-of-execution recursively until 1,000,000 total actors/fibers are created (only 10,000 for std::thread/std::async/pthread due to resource exhaustion); each returns its ordinal number, summed back up to the root; average time-per-unit measured with std::chrono::high_resolution_clock
claimed_speedup: fiber (16C/32T, work-stealing, tcmalloc): 0.05-0.09 us/fiber (average over 1,000,000) vs std::thread 52-73 us/thread and std::async 106-122 us/thread (average over 10,000, because 1,000,000 threads exhausted resources); ~580-1460x lower time-per-unit vs std::thread and ~1180-2440x vs std::async (derived from page data). Single-thread round-robin fiber (1C/1T): 1.69-1.79 us/fiber, still ~30-40x lower than std::thread (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc-6.3.1, variant=release, optimization=speed
hardware: dual Intel Xeon E5-2620v4 2.2GHz, 16 cores/32 threads, 64GB RAM, Linux x86_64
stars_or_usage: 511 stars on the standalone mirror; ships as part of the Boost C++ Libraries collection used industry-wide
tradeoffs: Cooperative user-space scheduling: a blocking syscall or CPU-bound fiber can stall all fibers on its worker thread unless paired with async I/O (e.g. Boost.Asio integration); best numbers require a non-default allocator (tcmalloc) and a work-stealing scheduler configuration; different programming model (fiber-per-task) than raw std::thread/std::async call sites.
caveats: Numbers come from Boost's own project documentation (first party), though the benchmark code itself (performance/thread/skynet_std.cpp and the fiber counterpart in the same repo) is public and the compiler/flags/hardware are all stated, meeting the tier-A bar despite the source being first-party. The raw ratio (>50x) looks extreme, but it is explained by mechanism (fiber creation/context switch avoids syscalls and stack-guard-page setup that std::thread/std::async incur) rather than a flawed methodology; std::thread could only be tested at 10,000 units instead of 1,000,000 due to OS resource exhaustion, so the two are not run at identical scale. Measurements were taken with gcc-6.3.1, an old compiler (circa 2017); the fiber library and hardware landscape have moved on since, and the doc gives no indication the numbers were re-run on newer toolchains.

name: utl::parallel (UTL ThreadPool)
workload: Four microbenchmark scenarios, 1000 tasks each: (1) small non-recursive tasks busy-waiting 0-100us, (2) large non-recursive tasks busy-waiting 1000-3000us, (3) shallow recursive tasks (0-100us with 70% chance of spawning+awaiting one more such task), (4) deep recursive tasks (0-100us with 49% chance of spawning+awaiting two more such tasks, averaging ~50 subtasks); reports ms/op and op/s relative to a serial baseline
claimed_speedup: Small non-recursive: utl::parallel::ThreadPool 573.3% vs std::async() 214.0% of serial speed (~2.7x faster than std::async, derived from page data). Large non-recursive: 597.0% vs 564.2% (~1.06x, roughly tied). Shallow recursive: 583.0% vs 161.1% (~3.6x faster than std::async; BS::thread_pool and progschj/ThreadPool deadlock entirely on this workload). Deep recursive: 565.1% vs 154.7% (~3.65x faster than std::async, derived from page data).
hardware: 6-core AMD Ryzen 5 5600H, hyper-threading disabled
tradeoffs: Uses a custom future type instead of std::future so recursive awaiting doesn't deadlock, so it is not a drop-in std::future replacement; ships as one module inside a larger multi-module header-only utility collection (UTL) rather than a standalone package; explicitly a niche tool for recursive/scatter-gather workloads, not a general vendor-optimized scheduler like TBB/OpenMP.
caveats: Author explicitly disclaims superiority over vendor-optimized frameworks (OpenMP/TBB). On large non-recursive tasks the advantage over std::async almost disappears (~1.06x) since thread-creation overhead is amortized; the large speedups are concentrated in small-task and recursive-task scenarios, exactly where std::async's per-call thread-spawn cost dominates. Benchmarked on a single consumer laptop CPU (Ryzen 5 5600H), not server-class hardware; this is the project's own README benchmark with no independent third-party reproduction found, though code, compiler, flags, and CPU model are all public and stated (meets Tier A bar on reproducibility grounds). Library itself is small (336 stars) and young.

name: CRoaring (Roaring Bitmaps)
baseline: std::unordered_set<uint32_t> and sorted std::vector<uint32_t> with STL set algorithms (std::set_intersection/union/difference, std::binary_search) from the standard library bundled with GCC 5.4; also an uncompressed bitset (the authors' portable C 'cbitset', same word-array layout as std::bitset/std::vector<bool>)
workload: 8 realistic integer-set datasets (CensusInc, CensusInc-sorted, Census1881, Census1881-sorted, Weather, Weather-sorted, Wikileaks, Wikileaks-sorted; 200 sets each, universe sizes 200K-4.3M): sequential iteration/cardinality, random-access membership queries at n/4, n/2, 3n/4, and 199 pairwise intersections/unions/differences/symmetric differences between successive sets. Reported as CPU cycles per input value.
claimed_speedup: Mixed by dataset and operation (CPU cycles per input value, Tables 4/6/7). vs C++ standard library containers: two-by-two intersections (Table 7a), sorted std::vector + std::set_intersection 7.84 vs Roaring 0.220 on CensusInc (~36x, derived from page data), 3.28 vs 0.090 on Census1881 (~36x, derived from page data), 4.15 vs 1.43 on Wikileaks (~2.9x, derived from page data); std::unordered_set 55.3 vs 0.220 on CensusInc (~251x, derived from page data), 0.480 vs 0.090 on Census1881 (~5.3x, derived from page data); unions (Table 7b) std::unordered_set 210 vs 0.270 on CensusInc (~778x, derived from page data). Membership queries (Table 6): Roaring beats std::vector + std::binary_search on every dataset (e.g. 63.6 vs 415 cycles on CensusInc), but std::unordered_set is faster than Roaring on CensusInc, CensusInc-sorted, Weather and Weather-sorted (e.g. 49.2 vs 63.6) and slower on Census1881 (38.2 vs 17.4). vs uncompressed bitset (cbitset): intersections 19.5 vs 0.090 on Census1881 (~217x, derived from page data), 33.0 vs 0.140 on Census1881-sorted (~236x, derived from page data), 26.4 vs 1.43 on Wikileaks (~18x, derived from page data); but on CensusInc/CensusInc-sorted/Weather the bitset is faster (CensusInc: bitset 0.120-0.130 vs Roaring 0.220-0.370 across the four set operations, ~1.7-3.1x, derived from page data). Bitset wins every membership query (2.36-3.74 vs Roaring 17.4-76.8 cycles). Memory (Table 4, bits/value): Roaring 15.1 vs bitset 524 on Census1881, 2.60 vs 5.66 on CensusInc, 0.340 vs 11.4 on Weather-sorted; std::vector uses 32 and std::unordered_set 195 bits/value on every dataset.
compiler_and_flags: GNU GCC 5.4, compiled with -O3 -march=native
hardware: Intel i7-6700 (Skylake, 3.4 GHz, 32KB L1d, 256KB L2/core, 8MB L3), 32GB DDR4-2133 dual-channel, single-threaded, Turbo Boost disabled, timed with rdtsc, results reproducible within 5%
stars_or_usage: 1,887 stars; used by Apache Doris, ClickHouse, Alibaba Tair, Redpanda, YDB, StarRocks
tradeoffs: Roaring wins decisively on memory and on set-algebra over sparse/clustered 32-bit integer sets, but loses to a plain uncompressed bitset on random-access membership queries (bitset has roughly an order of magnitude lower latency) and can lose on set-algebra for dense/small-universe datasets. Targets dynamic sparse 32-bit integer sets, not fixed-size dense bit flags, so it is not a general drop-in for std::bitset<N> or std::vector<bool>.
caveats: Results depend heavily on dataset and operation: Roaring loses to a plain bitset on dense datasets and on all membership queries, and loses to std::unordered_set on membership queries for 4 of 8 datasets. The bitset baseline is the authors' own 'cbitset' C library, not std::bitset/std::vector<bool>. The STL containers are literally the standard library that ships with GCC 5.4 (libstdc++ inferred from 'the standard C++ library bundled with our compiler' on Linux), which is from 2016. The paper's authors also maintain the library (Lemire et al., Software: Practice and Experience 2018), but the code, compiler, flags and CPU are all public.

name: plf::bitset (plf_bitsets)
workload: Full bitset test-suite exercised in a loop (set/reset/shift/index/etc.); separately, set_range/reset_range on a 128000-bit bitset over 10000 randomly chosen ranges per run.
claimed_speedup: Release (O2, AVX2): 24% (GCC)/20% (MSVC) faster overall test suite; 34,652%/67,612% faster set_range/reset_range; ~101%/98% faster left/right shift (GCC), 35%/22% (MSVC); 6%/204% faster set(pos,val); 3%/0% faster operator[]. Debug builds show much larger gaps (up to 428,127%/750,726% for set_range/reset_range).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.2 (nuwen mingw) and MSVC 2022; release build: O2, AVX2, C++23
hardware: Intel i7-9750H, Windows 10 (safe mode)
license: Computing For Good License v1.01 (non-OSI; zlib-style terms plus ethical field-of-use restrictions 4a-4e)
tradeoffs: plf::bitset omits std::bitset's from-string/from-ulong constructors; adds set_range/reset_range, range-based any/all/none/count, an allocation-free XOR swap, index-bounds-checking via a template flag, and a user-supplied-buffer variant (plf::bitsetb) not present in std::bitset.

The extreme set_range/reset_range percentages (up to ~677x) mostly reflect that std::bitset has no ranged-set primitive (callers loop bit-by-bit), so they are partly an algorithmic win rather than a raw constant-factor speedup; the overall test-suite numbers (~20-24%) better represent general use. Not every operation wins: MSVC's std::bitset to_string (which uses an intrinsic) beats plf, and the author says other operations perform about the same. Licensed under 'Computing For Good License v1.01' (zlib-like with ethical-use restrictions 4a-4e, not OSI-approved), so usability is 'reference'.

claimed_speedup: up to 8% faster rank and up to 16.5% faster select vs cs-poppy, at equal space overhead
compiler_and_flags: GCC 10.2, -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG (CMake 3.22.1)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (16 cores, up to 3.5 GHz), 64 GiB DDR4 RAM, Ubuntu 20.04.2 LTS; single core used (sequential experiments)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20; GPL-3.0 is more restrictive than MIT/BSD peers; adds rank/select operations that std::bitset/std::vector<bool> lack entirely, so it's an additive capability rather than a drop-in replacement; fastest variant relies on SIMD and -march=native.
caveats: std::bitset and std::vector<bool> have no native rank/select, so there is no direct std baseline for this functionality. The recorded baseline (cs-poppy, Zhou et al. SEA'13) is the field's standard compact rank/select structure, not a stdlib facility, which caps confidence. The gains are small: rank is roughly 8% faster (pasta-poppy and pasta-flat) and select is 16.5% faster (pasta-flatSIMD) vs cs-poppy at the same ~3.51% space overhead. Rank-only structures such as sdsl-v and rank9select answer rank faster but use 1.75-6.98x more space. The paper is peer-reviewed (SPIRE 2022, DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-20643-6_19), and reproduction scripts are public at github.com/pasta-toolbox/bit_vector_experiments. GPL-3.0 is a copyleft license.

name: better_bitset
workload: Find index of first set bit ('first_one') across bitsets of size 4-8192 bits, ~5 average one-bits per bitset, 1000 random bitsets per size, measured with Google Benchmark; the std::bitset side is a manual bit-by-bit loop using .test(i), since std::bitset has no built-in bit-scan for sizes above 64.
claimed_speedup: README claims 'improvements averaging 60x' versus the iterative std::bitset approach. benchmark/results.txt: N=8192: 953,294 ns (std::bitset .test(i) loop) vs 18,134 ns (better_bitset) = ~52.6x faster (derived from page data); N=1024: 128,450 vs 1,789 ns = ~71.8x (derived from page data); N=64: 6,349 vs 213 ns = ~29.8x (derived from page data); N=8: 701 vs 218 ns = ~3.2x (derived from page data); but N=4: 250 ns (std::bitset) vs 405 ns (better_bitset), so better_bitset is ~1.6x SLOWER there (derived from page data). The mean of the 13 per-size ratios is ~34x (derived from page data), below the README's 60x.
hardware: 20 logical CPUs @ ~3609.6 MHz (Google Benchmark auto-detected clock speed and cache sizes only; exact CPU model name not recorded)
tradeoffs: Not a drop-in replacement: only implements first_zero/first_one plus the common subset (all/any/none/count/size/set/reset/flip/to_string); lacks bitwise operators and the std::bitset reference-proxy type. Also smaller than std::bitset for sizes <=16 bits.
caveats: Small, unmaintained repo (last commit 2022, 8 stars). The benchmark is first-party and results.txt records no compiler or optimization flags (the CMakeLists set neither, so the build may not have been optimized), and names the CPU only by core count and clock speed. The std::bitset side is a naive bit-by-bit .test(i) loop written for the benchmark (standard std::bitset has no find-first operation; libstdc++'s non-standard _Find_first() was not used), so the speedup is mostly an algorithmic win over a strawman. better_bitset is slower at N=4. There is no LICENSE file, so the code can be studied but not safely reused.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch '"Bitset2" ClaasBontus header-only bitset benchmark std::bitset' surfaced https://github.com/MrElectrify/better_bitset; benchmark folder and results opened at github.com/MrElectrify/better_bitset/tree/master/benchmark

name: atomic_queue
workload: SPSC round-trip ping-pong: 2 threads exchange a 4-byte int counter 1,000,000 times via two queue instances (lowest-contention case); also an N-producer/N-consumer throughput scalability test moving 1,000,000 messages through one queue, run across AMD Ryzen 5950X, Ryzen 5825U, Intel i9-9900KS and Intel Xeon Gold 6132.
claimed_speedup: Ping-pong latency on Ryzen 5950X (SMT): AtomicQueue mean 42ns vs std::mutex 320ns (~7.6x lower); OptimistAtomicQueue 33ns (~9.7x lower). 1-producer/1-consumer throughput on 5950X: AtomicQueue ~142.7M msg/s vs std::mutex ~4.1M msg/s (~34x); OptimistAtomicQueue mean ~1.23B msg/s (stdev ~136M, max ~2.04B). With 2-16 producer/consumer pairs, OptimistAtomicQueue stays ~4-24x ahead of std::mutex (52.9M vs 13.0M msg/s at 2; 55.3M vs 2.3M at 16), while plain AtomicQueue is roughly at parity with std::mutex.
compiler_and_flags: gcc-14.2.0 (Ryzen 5950X/5825U); gcc-8.4.0 (legacy i9-9900KS/Xeon Gold 6132). Current Makefile gcc release flags: -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -falign-functions=64 -DNDEBUG -fno-stack-protector -fno-stack-clash-protection -fno-tree-ch -fno-move-loop-invariants -fno-plt -fno-math-errno -ffinite-math-only -pthread; benchmarks.cc is compiled with -std=c++17, which is appended after the base -std=c++14.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5950X and Ryzen 5825U (KDE Neon/Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8, mitigations=off); legacy: Intel i9-9900KS (Kubuntu 18.04) and Intel Xeon Gold 6132 (RHEL 6.10)
stars_or_usage: 1.9k stars; packaged in Conan Center and vcpkg
tradeoffs: Fixed capacity set at compile/construction time (ring buffer, no heap growth); no OS-blocking wait, only busy-spin (push/pop can't sleep, unsuitable for non-latency-critical code that wants to yield the CPU); atomic-element variants reserve a NIL sentinel value that must never be pushed; value-semantics only (copies/moves elements, no in-place references).
caveats: The 'std::mutex' baseline is atomic_queue's own fixed-size ring buffer guarded by std::mutex (AtomicQueueMutex), polled through try_push/try_pop retry loops. It is not std::queue with a condition variable. The ~1.23B msg/s 1P/1C OptimistAtomicQueue figure varies a lot (stdev ~136M, max ~2.04B). The page says throughput exceeds the inverse of latency on purpose, because the throughput loop has no dependency chains. Treat the 7.6-9.7x latency figures as the conservative claim. With 2+ producer/consumer pairs on the 5950X, plain AtomicQueue is roughly at parity with std::mutex: std::mutex leads at 2 pairs (13.0M vs 10.1M msg/s) and ties at 4. Only OptimistAtomicQueue keeps a large throughput lead under contention.

name: contention_free_shared_mutex (AlexeyAB/object_threadsafe safe_ptr library)
workload: Concurrent read/write locking benchmark (bench_contfree / benchmark / CDS_test folders) comparing contention_free_shared_mutex<> to std::shared_mutex under multi-threaded mixed read/write contention on a shared object; exact operation counts and thread counts are shown only in chart images in the README, not as text/tables.
claimed_speedup: README headline: "contention_free_shared_mutex<> - 10 X times faster than std::shared_mutex". CodeProject Article 2 (archived), 16 threads on Xeon E5-2660 v3, std::map guarded by the lock: 0% modifications 34.60 Mops (contfree_safe_ptr<map>) vs 2.44 Mops (safe_ptr<map, std::shared_mutex>), stated as 14x; 15% modifications 5.16 vs 0.74 Mops, stated as 7x. The README charts (90% update/5% insert/5% delete, 20 usec forced delay, 2x Xeon E5-2686 v4) show about 1.9 vs about 0.4 MOps at 64 threads (~5x, read approximately from the chart image) and near-parity at 16 threads or fewer.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 6.3.0 on Linux, g++ -std=c++14 -pthread -O3 (bench_contfree/Makefile). The article also offers an MSVS 2015 build, but the published run command (numactl ... ./benchmark 16) is Linux.
hardware: Article numbers: single Intel Xeon E5-2660 v3 2.6 GHz, 16 threads (numactl --cpunodebind=0). README charts: 2x Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 2.3 GHz (36 cores/72 threads).
tradeoffs: contention_free_shared_mutex shards locking state per-thread to avoid contention, which increases memory usage relative to std::shared_mutex; safe_ptr<>/contfree_safe_ptr<> wrap objects and change access syntax (operator-> based locking) rather than being a drop-in mutex replacement; recursive-lock semantics differ from std::shared_mutex.
caveats: First-party benchmark from 2017-era articles. The 10x headline is a middle value: the article shows 14x at 0% writes and 7x at 15% writes, and the lock is contention-free only up to 36 threads (template parameter). Above that it acts as an exclusive lock. The README's real-app chart (20 usec delay) shows parity up to 16 threads and ~5x only at 64 threads. CodeProject's live page now redirects to a lander, so the evidence is the Wayback copy. The last commit is 2020-04-13, so the project is unmaintained.

name: eventpp::SpinLock (eventpp GeneralThreading policy)
workload: EventQueue enqueue/process microbenchmark: N enqueue threads and N process threads (1 to 16) moving 10M events across 100 event types/listeners, protected by either std::mutex or eventpp::SpinLock as the Threading::Mutex policy.
claimed_speedup: 10M events, 100 event types/listeners (doc/benchmark.md): 1 enqueue/1 process thread: SpinLock 1303 ms vs std::mutex 1824 ms (~1.4x faster, derived from page data); 1/3: 3186 vs 2989 ms (SpinLock slower); 2/2: 3049 vs 3151 ms (slightly faster); 4/4: 1659 vs 1657 ms (tie); 16/16: 1891 vs 708 ms (SpinLock ~2.7x SLOWER, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: MinGW GCC 11.3.0 (stated default compiler for this table; MSVC 2022 also used elsewhere in the same doc for other tables; optimization flags not stated)
hardware: Intel Core i5-8300H @ 2.30GHz, 16GB RAM, Windows 10 (per doc/benchmark.md, described by the author as 'pretty medium to low end')
tradeoffs: SpinLock busy-waits (burns CPU) instead of blocking via the kernel; degrades badly under thread oversubscription; only a real win when thread count is at or below the physical core count; not a safe general drop-in replacement for std::mutex.
caveats: First-party benchmark. The doc states the CPU model and compilers but not the optimization flags or build type, so the tier is capped at C. name: parallel-hashmap (phmap)
workload: Inserting up to 100 million key/value pairs (two 8-byte integers) into phmap::flat_hash_map vs std::unordered_map, per the project's online design writeup.
claimed_speedup: Writeup: "the Abseil flat_hash_map is significantly faster that the default stl implementation, typically about three times faster". That quote is literally about absl::flat_hash_map vs VS2017 std::unordered_map. phmap's own flat/parallel maps are graphed as nearly indistinguishable from it, and parallel_flat_hash_map is slightly slower for small tables and converges above ~80M values. Repo raw data (benchmark/results/output_stl_flat_par), 100M random inserts: std::unordered_map 48.38 s vs phmap::flat_hash_map 14.41 s vs phmap::parallel_flat_hash_map 14.47 s, ~3.4x (derived from repo data).
compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2017 MSVC (cl -EHsc -DNDEBUG -O2 per benchmark/Makefile), 64-bit, run from Cygwin
tradeoffs: flat_hash_map/flat_hash_set move keys and values in memory, so pointers/iterators are invalidated on mutation, unlike std::unordered_map's node-based stability; node_hash_map avoids that at some speed/memory cost; the parallel_* variants add multithreading support and lower peak resize memory at the cost of being slightly slower for small tables. The author now steers new users to the C++20 successor repo 'gtl' (also by greg7mdp, not filed separately here since it shares the same design and no independent benchmark was found for it).
caveats: The '~3x faster' sentence in the writeup refers to Abseil's flat_hash_map, of which phmap is a header-only derivative. The phmap-vs-std number comes from the repo's raw results CSV and graphs, not from a sentence. No CPU model is stated anywhere, so it is capped at Tier C. name: reckless
workload: Caller-side log-call latency in four scenarios. (1) Single-threaded periodic calls that never fill the buffer. (2) A call burst that fills the buffer. (3) Disk I/O: 2048 log entries interleaved with writing 64 GiB of data. (4) A Mandelbrot computation that logs ~1M lines with 1-8 worker threads (total runtime over 100 runs, overhead vs no-op). Baselines are std::fstream (std::flush after each line) and fprintf (fflush after each call), plus spdlog, g3log and Boost.Log.
claimed_speedup: Relative average call latency (reckless = 1.00). Periodic calls: fstream 41.32, stdio 43.77, spdlog 40.85, boost_log 67.42, g3log 78.19. Call burst: spdlog 1.93, fstream 2.36, stdio 2.55. Disk I/O: stdio 17.01, spdlog 23.82, fstream 5719.93. Mandelbrot overhead: single thread fstream 10.73, stdio 12.21, spdlog 9.21; 8 threads fstream 4.62, stdio 3.70. The page concludes: 'For low loads, the speed advantage over a simple fprintf can be a factor of 40.'
compiler_and_flags: gcc 7.3.0 (stated on the benchmark page). The benchmarks are built with tup (benchmarks/Tupfile.lua + Tuprules.lua), which on Linux compiles with g++ -O3 -ggdb3 -std=c++11 -Wall -Werror unless DEBUG=yes (then -O0). The page itself does not restate the flags.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 2700X @ 3.7GHz, 8 cores (SMT off); Samsung 970 EVO 1TB SSD (+ WD Red 3TB HDD for disk-I/O scenario); 32GB RAM; Linux kernel 4.14.65
tradeoffs: Async design allows passing raw pointers to the background writer thread for speed, at the cost of dangling-pointer risk if misused; trades some floating-point formatting precision for performance; writes are backgrounded/batched rather than immediate, with a configurable buffer size trading latency spikes against memory use.
caveats: The benchmark is first-party. reckless is asynchronous (formatting and writing happen on a background thread), while the fstream/stdio baselines flush after every line. So the win is caller-side latency under an async-vs-synchronous-flush design, not raw I/O throughput. The figures use 2019-era versions of the competitors (spdlog 1.3.1, g3log 1.3.2, Boost 1.65). GitHub's license detector reports NOASSERTION, but LICENSE.txt is standard MIT text. The last commit on master is 2021-04-10 (a 'next' branch has 2022-07-17 commits); the repo's pushed_at of 2023-10-22 matches no branch head.

name: SLEEF (SIMD Library for Evaluating Elementary Functions)
baseline: <cmath> (scalar libm, represented in the paper by FDLIBM as the reference scalar implementation)
workload: Reciprocal throughput (ns per call) of 256-bit vectorized double-precision SLEEF 3.4 (plus Vector-libm and Intel SVML) vs scalar FDLIBM 5.3. A single-threaded tight loop makes 10^10 calls over pre-generated, uniformly random arguments in each listed domain. The calling loop was compiled without optimization so calls are not elided (the libraries use their -O3 flags), and it is timed with clock_gettime.
claimed_speedup: Table 2, reciprocal throughput in ns per call, 1-ulp variants. SLEEF is the 256-bit AVX2 vectorized function (each call evaluates 4 doubles); FDLIBM 5.3 is scalar (1 value per call). sin [0,1e+100]: FDLIBM 162.3 vs SLEEF 48.79 (~3.3x per call). cos [0,1e+100]: 162.1 vs 50.38 (~3.2x). tan [0,1e+100]: 177.0 vs 48.82 (~3.6x). log [0,1e+300]: 31.66 vs 15.46 (~2.0x). exp [-700,700]: 12.19 vs 7.663 (~1.6x). pow: 69.40 vs 55.53 (~1.25x). On the fast-path domain [0.4,0.5], scalar FDLIBM is FASTER per call (sin 4.927 vs 11.43, cos 11.42 vs 13.75, tan 7.819 vs 17.30), as it is for acos (12.07 vs 16.09) and atan (10.16 vs 22.12). Per element (dividing by 4 lanes), SLEEF is faster in every 1-ulp row. (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: SLEEF and FDLIBM compiled with gcc-7.3.0 -O3 -mavx2 -mfma; Vector-libm compiled with gcc-7.3.0 -O3 -march=native -ftree-vectorize -ftree-vectorizer-verbose=1 -fno-math-errno; SVML via Intel C Compiler 19 with -fimf-max-error=1.0/4.0
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 CPU @ 3.40GHz, Turbo Boost disabled (physical PC, no VM)
tradeoffs: Vectorized code takes the slow path for a whole SIMD register if any lane needs it; library offers a 1-ULP and a faster 3.5-ULP accuracy tier as a speed/accuracy tradeoff; on narrow argument domains the scalar-equivalent speed roughly ties FDLIBM rather than beating it, the win is concentrated in wide-domain/branchy cases and true vector (multi-lane) throughput.
caveats: Table 2 compares SLEEF's 4-wide AVX2 vector functions against scalar FDLIBM. It is not a like-for-like scalar replacement of std::sin/std::exp: the gains need vectorized call sites, and SLEEF's scalar entry points are not in the table. Per call, FDLIBM beats vector SLEEF on narrow-domain sin/cos/tan and on acos/atan. FDLIBM is a reference libm, not glibc's libm or the libm behind libstdc++/libc++/MSVC <cmath>. The benchmark loop was built unoptimized for every library alike. The sleef.org benchmark page compares only against SVML. The Table 2 harness for FDLIBM is not in the repo.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "vectorized math library faster than std::exp std::sin benchmark C++" led to the SLEEF arXiv paper; repo confirmed via gh api repos/shibatch/sleef

verification.tier_reason: A peer-reviewed paper (IEEE TPDS vol. 31 no. 6, June 2020; arXiv 2001.09258) gives Table 2 reciprocal throughputs for SLEEF vs scalar FDLIBM 5.3, with gcc-7.3.0 -O3 -mavx2 -mfma on an i7-6700 with Turbo off. The Table 2 harness is not published: SLEEF 3.4.0's src/libm-benchmarks has only SLEEF/SVML benches, not FDLIBM, and master no longer has that directory. So it is not A.
verification.notes: The record misread Table 2. Its 'narrow domain parity, sin 11.43 vs 11.41' pairs two SLEEF cells (the [0.4,0.5] and [0,6.28] rows); the actual FDLIBM value for narrow-domain sin is 4.927, so FDLIBM wins per call there. The record also hid that the comparison is SIMD-vs-scalar. The tier stays B; the verdict is downgrade because the claim needed substantive correction. The metadata (BSL-1.0, 853 stars, last commit 2025-12-25, active) is correct.

A batch/array API (1M elements per call) for sin/cos/sincos/atan2 is measured separately.

name: libart (Adaptive Radix Tree)
baseline: red-black tree (the ART paper's own in-memory red-black-tree implementation, algorithmically what std::map/std::set are built on, but not literally libstdc++/libc++/MSVC's std::map)
workload: single-threaded lookups of existing random 32-bit-integer keys in an index of 65K, 16M, and 256M keys, both dense and sparse key distributions (also a 12-thread/8-way-software-pipelined variant at 16M keys), from the ART paper's micro-benchmarks
claimed_speedup: From the ART paper's Fig. 10 (single-threaded lookups of random existing 32-bit keys; derived from page data: read off bar chart, approximate; measures the paper authors' ART, not libart): 65K keys: ART ~108M lookups/s dense, ~35M/s sparse vs red-black tree ~7.5M/s (~14x dense, ~4.7x sparse); 16M keys: ART ~20M/s dense, ~10.7M/s sparse vs RB ~1.2M/s (~17x / ~9x); 256M keys: ART ~10.1M/s dense, ~6.8M/s sparse vs RB ~0.65M/s (~15x / ~10x). The paper's chained hash table beats ART on sparse keys at every size; in Fig. 11 (16M keys, 12 threads, 8-way software pipelining) ART dense ~195M/s vs hash table ~132M/s, but ART sparse ~110M/s is slower than the hash table. The paper's 1.6-1.7x (ART) and 1.2x (HT) figures are speedups from software pipelining, not ART-vs-HT ratios.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.6 (optimization flags not stated in the text)
hardware: Intel Core i7 3930K, 6 cores/12 threads, 3.2GHz (3.8GHz turbo), 12MB shared L3 cache, 32GB quad-channel DDR3-1600 RAM, Linux 3.2 x86-64
stars_or_usage: 836 stars; the ART algorithm (the paper's implementation, not libart) was integrated into the HyPer main-memory database per the paper
tradeoffs: keys are limited to fixed-width binary-comparable encodings (signed integers, floats, and strings all need a transform to sort correctly bitwise); path compression and lazy expansion are required to bound worst-case space to ~52 bytes/key; libart (this repo) is an independent open-source C99 implementation of the paper's algorithm, not the authors' original benchmark artifact
caveats: libart has no benchmarks of its own (repo has only src/ and tests/); all numbers come from the ART paper (ICDE 2013), which measured the authors' own ART and own red-black tree ('two textbook data structures'), not libart and not libstdc++/libc++/MSVC std::map; values are read off bar charts; the paper removed path compression for the 32-bit-key micro-benchmarks; the paper's hash table beats ART on sparse keys; libart last commit 2021-02-11 (abandoned).

workload: Fisher-Yates shuffle of std::vector<uint64_t> (10,000 and 1,000,000 elements) driven by std::mt19937_64. std::shuffle is compared with batched_random::shuffle_2, which draws two bounded indices from one 64-bit random word using multiplication-based, nearly-divisionless bounded generation.
claimed_speedup: vs std::shuffle with std::mt19937_64. Apple M2, Apple/LLVM 15 (libc++): 12.4 vs 2.4 ns/element at 10,000 elements and 12.0 vs 2.5 ns/element at 1,000,000 elements (~4.8-5.2x, derived from page data; the author says 'four to five times faster'). Linux, Intel CPU (model not stated), GCC 12 (libstdc++): 2.2 vs 1.7 ns/element at 10,000 and 3.5 vs 2.7 ns/element at 1,000,000 (~1.3x, derived from page data; the author says 'about 30% faster').
compiler_and_flags: Apple/LLVM 15 (M2 run); GCC 12 (Linux run); -std=c++17 -O3 per the linked benchmark Makefile
hardware: Apple M2 MacBook; Linux machine with an Intel processor whose model is not stated
tradeoffs: Only benefits shuffles driven by a 64-bit-output RNG (e.g. std::mt19937_64); speed advantage shrinks for very large arrays and grows for small/medium ones; adds an extra header dependency vs calling std::shuffle directly.
caveats: The blog numbers were measured with the 2024 prototype header (batched_random::shuffle_2 in lemire/Code-used-on-Daniel-Lemire-s-blog/2024/08/16), the direct predecessor of this repo (created 2025-09). They are not from this repo's current batched_random::shuffle. The gain depends on the standard library: ~4.8-5.2x against libc++ but only ~1.3x against libstdc++, which already uses Lemire's nearly-divisionless bounded method. The peer-reviewed paper (arXiv:2408.06213, SPE 55(1) 2024) reports 1.4-4.7x (Xeon Gold 6338, LLVM 16) and 1.5-3.9x (Apple M2, Apple/LLVM 14). Those paper numbers compare a C implementation against the authors' own unbatched C Fisher-Yates that already uses an efficient bounded-integer method, not against std::shuffle. The header requires a 64-bit URBG and uses static_assert to check it. The repo is dual-licensed MIT and Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception.

name: Random123
workload: Single-chip raw random byte-stream generation throughput (GB/s) and cycles-per-byte, counter-based generators (Philox, Threefry, ARS) vs conventional PRNGs including the C++0x std::mt19937_64.
claimed_speedup: ARS-7 (AES-NI hardware-accelerated): 11.1 GB/s vs std::mt19937_64: 6.1 GB/s (~1.8x, derived from page data) on the Intel CPU tested; Threefry-4x64-20 (no special hardware needed): 6.4 GB/s vs 6.1 GB/s (~1.05x, derived from page data, i.e. only marginally faster without AES-NI)
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.5.3 (Intel CPU build); optimization flags not stated in the paper
hardware: 3.07GHz quad-core Intel Xeon X5667 (Westmere)
tradeoffs: Counter-based API (application manages key + counter explicitly) is a different programming model than a stateful std::mt19937 engine, so it is not a drop-in engine substitute without an adapter; the standout CPU speedup (ARS-7) needs AES-NI hardware support -- without it, gains over std::mt19937_64 on CPU are small; largest wins shown in the paper are on GPU, not directly relevant to a CPU std::mt19937 comparison.
caveats: Peer-reviewed paper (Salmon, Moraes, Dror & Shaw, 'Parallel Random Numbers: As Easy as 1,2,3', SC11) with a benchmark table (Table 2) that states CPU model and compiler but not flags. The hardware dates from 2011 (Westmere Xeon X5667). On the CPU, only the AES-NI generators (ARS-5 17.8 GB/s, ARS-7 11.1 GB/s) and Threefry-4x64-12 (11.2 GB/s) clearly beat std::mt19937_64 (6.1 GB/s). The recommended portable Threefry-4x64-20 is roughly a tie (6.4 GB/s), and the Philox variants are slower on the CPU (for example Philox4x32-10 at 3.4 GB/s and Philox4x64-10 at 3.9 GB/s). The large wins in the paper are on GPUs, where there is no C++ std baseline. GitHub's license detector reports NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is standard BSD-3-Clause text.

name: plf::colony (plf::hive)
workload: Independent microbenchmark suite (fill/back-insertion, linear search, random insert, randomized iterate-and-erase at 1%/50% erasure probability, sort, destruction) across element sizes from 8B to 4096B on GCC/libstdc++.
claimed_speedup: "three orders of magnitude faster than the vector and deque" at 1% iterate-and-erase with 1024B elements; "the colony in this case is about 361'143 times faster than the vector!" at 50% erasure, largest configuration (verbatim from post). For fill/back-insertion of 8B elements the post says "almost three times slower is the colony" vs vector-with-reserve (32B: "almost the same with less margin"). Linear search: colony "even 50% slower than the list container".
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.9.4, -std=c++11 -march=native -O2
hardware: Intel Core i7-4770 @ 3.4GHz, Gentoo Linux
tradeoffs: Unordered container: element insertion order is not preserved and elements are not indexable by position like vector's operator[]; higher per-element memory overhead (skip-field metadata) than vector; key advantage is that erase() never invalidates other iterators/pointers/references (unlike vector/deque), which is what makes bulk random erasure O(1) per element instead of O(n).
caveats: Benchmark dated 2017 on GCC 4.9.4 (dated compiler); the headline 361,143x figure is specific to a 50%-random-erasure iterate/erase workload on large (multi-KB) elements at whatever container size the author's graph reached, and reflects colony's O(1) erase vs. vector/deque's O(n) erase-and-shift -- an asymptotic-complexity artifact, not a representative 'typical workload' multiplier; for simple sequential fill of small/medium elements the same post reports colony as slower than std::vector. Only libstdc++ (GCC) was exercised in this post, not libc++ or MSVC STL. The library's own site (plflib.org/colony.htm, colony v6.11, GCC 9.2 x64, Intel Xeon E3-1241 Haswell, -O2 -march=native, benchmark source in the colony downloads section) shows qualitatively consistent rankings (colony/list leading insertion and erasure, vector leading iteration) but presents numbers as graph images rather than machine-readable text, so it was used only as corroboration, not the primary citation. The library has since been forked/renamed to plf::hive (github.com/mattreecebentley/plf_hive, 179 stars, also active) to track the pending std::hive standardization proposal (P0447); both repos are maintained in parallel by the same author and the cited benchmark evidence applies to both implementations.

claimed_speedup: Faster than nlohmann::json at parsing: 2.2x on twitter.json (402.89 vs 182.76 op/s), 2.4x on apache_builds.json (2,134.76 vs 881.03 op/s), and about 4x on strings.json and numbers.json (derived from page data). RapidJSON beats utl::json on parsing on every file except strings.json: numbers.json 1.29-1.45x, twitter.json 2.07-2.22x, apache_builds.json 1.63-1.72x, database.json 1.30-1.40x. name: CDRC atomic_weak_ptr (concurrent_deferred_rc)

claimed_speedup: CDRC atomic weak pointers vs just::thread: 4.2x faster at P=8 and 10x faster at P=192 (paper Sec. 5.2). At P=1 (off-plot), the paper says the hand-tuned 'original' manual-reclamation queue is 4.5x faster than CDRC and 67x faster than just::thread, which puts CDRC ~15x ahead of just::thread at P=1 (derived from page data: 67/4.5). name: BlockQuicksort
workload: Sorting arrays of random 32-bit ints, 10-dimensional double Vectors (Euclidean-norm comparator), and 21-field int Records, measured as elements sorted per second, against GCC's std::sort.
claimed_speedup: More than 80% more elements sorted per second than GCC's std::sort on random ints. Section 4: optimized BlockQuicksort needs ~45 ns/element vs 85 ns/element for std::sort at n=2^28 (+88%), and the duplicate-check variant is almost twice as fast on random ints in [0, sqrt n]. Figure 7 shows smaller but positive gains on Vector and Record for the BlockQS (mo-sqrt n, dc) variant. std::sort wins only on sorted or almost-sorted inputs.
compiler_and_flags: GNU g++ 4.8.4, -O3 -march=native
hardware: Intel Core i5-2500K @ 3.30GHz, 4 cores, 32KB L1 i/d, 256KB L2/core, 6MB shared L3, 16GB RAM, Ubuntu 14.04.4 64-bit
stars_or_usage: 40 stars; algorithm published in ACM Journal of Experimental Algorithmics (2019) and cited as the 'closest sequential competitor' baseline in the IPS4o paper
tradeoffs: In-place but not stable; block size (default 128) needs tuning per data type; branch-misprediction-avoidance technique now widely reused (e.g. pdqsort, PPQSort) under more permissive licenses than this repo's GPL-3.0.
caveats: Repo unmaintained since Nov 2021; the std::sort compared against is a bundled copy of GCC 4.7.2's libstdc++ implementation (see paper footnote 3), not necessarily the std::sort of the g++ 4.8.4 compiler used to build the test; no libc++ or MSVC STL comparison.

claimed_speedup: spreadsort ~1.94x faster than std::sort on 100M random 64-bit ints (8.2154s vs 4.2248s); the in-repo benchmark_numbers.cpp table on the same page gives 8.21s vs 4.26s (~1.93x). ~2.57x faster on 10M random strings (6.2442s vs 2.4323s); ~1.62x faster on 100M 8-byte objects with a heavy comparator (8.25s vs 5.10s). spreadsort is slower than std::sort on fully reverse-sorted ints (1.87s vs 1.36s).

name: IPS⁴o (In-place Parallel Super Scalar Samplesort)
workload: Sorting 2^10 to 2^32 uniformly-distributed 64-bit floating point elements (also Pair/Quartet/100Bytes records and skewed distributions), sequential and multi-core, on four different server machines.
claimed_speedup: Sequential (Table 1 of arXiv 2009.13569, average slowdowns relative to the fastest algorithm per input, averaged over the four machines and inputs of at least 2^18 bytes): I1S4o (sequential IPS4o) vs std::sort, Total: double 1.20 vs 2.47, uint64 1.46 vs 2.95, uint32 1.78 vs 3.93, Pair 1.52 vs 2.45; Uniform: double 1.08 vs 2.43, uint64 1.35 vs 3.02, uint32 1.67 vs 4.02. By Total, I1S4o is about 2.06x (double), 2.02x (uint64), 2.21x (uint32) and 1.61x (Pair) faster than std::sort (derived from page data). Fig. 11 (Uniform uint64) shows std::sort off the plot, above I1S4o, on all four machines. Parallel: the paper reports no parallel speedup against std::sort; its parallel speedups (8.37 on A1x16, 40.92 on A1x64, 20.91 on I4x20, 17.49 on I2x16) are relative to sequential I1S4o.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 7.5.0, -march=native -O3
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (A1x16); AMD EPYC Rome 7702P (A1x64); 2x Intel Xeon E5-2683 v4 (I2x16); 4x Intel Xeon Gold 6138 (I4x20)
stars_or_usage: 135 stars (canonical repo); used as the reference sequential/parallel sorting baseline in numerous follow-up algorithm-engineering papers and benchmark suites (e.g. PPQSort)
tradeoffs: Needs C++14; parallel mode requires OpenMP or std::thread plus TBB and 16-byte atomic compare-and-exchange support (or -mcx16/libatomic); does not compile on Windows; least advantage on already-sorted or low-cardinality inputs where n<=2^15.
caveats: Numbers come from the peer-reviewed ESA 2017 paper (Section 5, Figures 6-8), which used the older SaschaWitt/ips4o code. The ips4o/ips4o repo contains no benchmark code. A separate ips4o/ips4o-benchmark-suite (GPL-3.0) has a std::sort target but is not linked from the repo README and matches the later 4-machine journal version. ips4o/ips4o is a GitHub fork of the now-deprecated SaschaWitt/ips4o and is the maintained successor. The 1.86x std::sort factor applies at n=2^32; DualPivot beats IS4o on AlmostSorted input by 1.70x, and IS4o is slower than BlockQuicksort for n<=2^15. The parallel advantage shrinks to ~1.41x on the 4-socket Intel4S machine. [retier] Table 1 values are average slowdown factors, not direct timings. std::sort is the sequential GCC introsort, so no parallel-vs-std::sort figure exists in the paper.

name: LearnedSort
workload: Sorting 50 million double-precision keys drawn from 8 distributions (Uniform, Exponential, Mixture of Gaussians, Zipf 0.75, TwoDups, Sorted, ReverseSorted, Identical), measured with Google Benchmark, comparing LearnedSort (a CDF-model-based sort) against std::sort, SkaSort, IS4o, BlockQuicksort, and Radix Sort.
claimed_speedup: Approximately 4.3x faster than GCC std::sort on Uniform data (~1150ms vs ~5000ms) and similarly ~4x on Exponential/Gaussian/Zipf/TwoDups distributions; roughly 15-20x faster on Sorted/ReverseSorted/Identical data (~50-60ms vs ~750-1000ms), per the README's bar chart
compiler_and_flags: GCC 9.3.0-10ubuntu2; CMake Release build with -O3 -march=native -fno-strict-overflow -mavx (CMakeLists.txt)
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6150 CPU @ 2.70GHz, 376GB RAM, Ubuntu 20.04 (kernel 5.4.0-26-generic)
stars_or_usage: 81 stars; published as 'The Case for a Learned Sorting Algorithm', SIGMOD 2020
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0 is a heavier copyleft obligation than most sort peers here; only supports numeric keys without payloads or string keys per the README's stated Limitations; training the CDF model adds setup cost that is not amortized on small inputs.
caveats: The README gives no benchmark numbers in text. The speedups were read off the bar chart (plots/perf_charts.png), so they are visual estimates, not exact printed figures. On Sorted, ReverseSorted and Identical inputs, IS4o is as fast as or faster than LearnedSort. The README says LearnedSort handles only numeric keys: no payloads (records) and no string keys. No commits since 2021; this is an unmaintained academic research prototype.
found_via: Web search 'SIMD sort faster than std::sort' / 'Learned Sort Kristo Kraska speedup std::sort benchmark'; opened anikristo/LearnedSort README.md and downloaded+viewed plots/perf_charts.png directly

verification.tier_reason: perf_charts.png plots LearnedSort vs Std::sort on 50M keys. The in-repo benchmark src/main_synth.cc (Google Benchmark, StdSort target) is built by CMakeLists.txt in Release with -O3 -march=native -mavx. The README states GCC 9.3.0 and the Xeon Gold 6150 machine; the work was also peer-reviewed at SIGMOD 2020.
verification.notes: The chart confirms the estimates: Uniform ~1130ms vs ~5000ms (~4.4x), other random distributions ~4.2-4.6x, and Sorted/Reverse/Identical ~50ms vs ~750-1000ms. The repo was transferred from learnedsystems/LearnedSort (that URL redirects here). Metadata verified: GPL-3.0, 81 stars, not a fork, last commit 2021-08-20 (abandoned).

name: x86-simd-sort (numpy/x86-simd-sort)
workload: Sorting an array of custom C++ Point structs (3D float/double coordinates) via object_qsort vs std::sort, sorted by one coordinate, Manhattan distance, Euclidean distance, or Chebyshev distance, measured with Google Benchmark on an AVX-512 capable processor.
claimed_speedup: object_qsort up to 5x faster for 32-bit key type and about 4x for 64-bit key type when sorting by one struct member; up to 10x faster when sorting by Euclidean distance
hardware: unspecified x86 processor with AVX-512 support
stars_or_usage: 1.0k stars; used as a submodule by NumPy (np.sort/argsort/partition) and PyTorch (torch.sort), integrated into OpenJDK, used by Alibaba GRAPE and OceanBase
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512 or AVX2; object_qsort needs O(N) extra memory for key/index arrays; speedup is highly dependent on the struct/key definition, README itself recommends benchmarking per use case rather than assuming the headline numbers.
caveats: The README does not state the CPU model, compiler or flags for the object_qsort chart, only 'a processor with AVX-512'. Benchmark code is in benchmarks/bench-objsort.hpp (run with --benchmark_filter=*obj*). Numbers are first-party and not from an independent third party. object_qsort needs O(N) extra space for keys and indexes. An independent 2023 analysis (Voultapher sort-research-rs, intel_avx512 writeup) reported worse-than-O(N log N) scaling of the AVX-512 qsort on a random_p5 pattern; this may be fixed in later releases.
found_via: GitHub/web search 'SIMD sort faster than std::sort' and 'x86-simd-sort Intel AVX-512 quicksort faster than std::sort'; confirmed via gh api repo metadata and a direct read of README.md and src/README.md
GitHub: gh search repos "quicksort SIMD" / gh search repos "x86-simd-sort"

verification.tier_reason: The README gives object_qsort vs std::sort numbers, and in-repo benchmark code (benchmarks/bench-objsort.hpp) exists. The README states only 'a processor with AVX-512', with no CPU model, compiler or flags, so tier A fails. The numbers are first-party and not peer-reviewed, so tier B also fails.
verification.notes: claimed_speedup matches the README text exactly (up to 5x for 32-bit, ~4x for 64-bit, up to 10x for Euclidean distance). Metadata verified: BSD-3-Clause, 1,027 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-06-25 (active). A third-party benchmark of the primitive qsort vs std::sort exists at sort-research-rs, but its std::sort numbers were not extracted here.

corrected_fields.caveats: README does not state the exact CPU model or compiler flags used for the object_qsort chart, only 'a processor with AVX-512'. Numbers come from the project's own README, not an independent third party.

name: poor-circle/radix_sort
workload: benchmark/benchmark.cpp: 1e6, 1e7, 1e8 and 1e9 uniformly random int, uint64, pair<int,uint32> and pair<uint64,uint64> (first-key) elements, 5 rounds averaged. Covers std::sort, std::stable_sort and radix_sort, both sequential and with std::execution::par. The README headline uses 1e9 int32.
claimed_speedup: README, 1 billion int32: radix_sort 6402ms vs std::sort 91407ms (README says '14.28x faster than std::sort') and vs std::stable_sort 82896ms (~12.9x). The README sets the parallel figure (radix_sort(par) 2603ms) only against single-threaded std::sort. benchmark/benchmark_output.txt shows std::sort(par) at 12537ms, so parallel against parallel is ~4.8x. The gain is smaller for wider keys. At 1e9 elements single-threaded it is ~5.2x for uint64 (17831ms vs 91867ms) and ~2.9x for pair<uint64,uint64> (33830ms vs 96751ms). In parallel on pair<uint64,uint64>, radix_sort(par) is slightly slower than std::sort(par) (24608ms vs 23532ms). The README headline range is '2.5-14.3x faster than std::sort'.
compiler_and_flags: Microsoft Visual C++ 2022, release mode (per benchmark/benchmark_output.txt); exact compiler flags not stated and no project file in repo
hardware: Intel Core i9-9900K @ 4.7GHz, DDR4-3000MHz RAM
tradeoffs: LSD radix sort restricted to keys with a defined 'radix trait' (integers, floats, pointers, pairs, user structs via traits) rather than arbitrary-comparator sorting like std::sort; needs an O(n) auxiliary buffer (user-suppliable).
caveats: Single-author project, unmaintained since Jan 2022. Only MSVC STL was tested (no libstdc++/libc++), and exact MSVC flags are not stated. The README's parallel figure sets parallel radix_sort against sequential std::sort; against std::sort(par) the win is ~4.8x for int32. The speedup falls for 64-bit and pair keys, and parallel radix_sort is slightly slower than std::sort(par) on pair<uint64,uint64>.

name: quadsort
workload: From the wolfsort bench.c: std::stable_sort vs quadsort vs timsort on 100,000 elements (32/64/128-bit) across 11 distributions (random, random%100, ascending, ascending saw, pipe organ, descending, descending saw, random tail, random half, ascending tiles, bit reversal), 100 samples with best and average reported. A second run covers random arrays of 1-4096 32-bit items (weighted repetitions, 50 samples).
claimed_speedup: ~2.4x faster than std::stable_sort (g++ 7.5 libstdc++) on random arrays of 513-1024 32-bit ints: best 0.005664s vs 0.013871s (weighted benchmark, 50 samples). Across random arrays of 1-4096 items the gain is ~2.0-4.9x. The README's 100,000-element per-distribution data table labels its rows 'fluxsort', not quadsort, although the bar graph says quadsort. That table shows ~4.1x for ascending saw and ~5.5x for pipe organ, and ~15-16x only for fully ascending or descending input. It is slower than std::stable_sort on bit reversal, which the graph also shows for quadsort. The earlier '~16x ascending-saw / ~10x pipe-organ' figures are not supported.
compiler_and_flags: g++ -O3 -w -fpermissive (GCC 7.5.0, WSL2/Ubuntu 18.04); a separate run used clang -O3 (clang 10)
tradeoffs: Stable, needs O(n) swap buffer like std::stable_sort; branchless design is tuned for GCC on x86 — author notes a 2-3x slowdown for the branchless merge/small-sort routines when compiled with clang instead of gcc.
caveats: First-party benchmark (the author's wolfsort suite, src/bench.c), not independently replicated. The CPU/hardware is never stated, only WSL2/Ubuntu 18.04 with GCC 7.5.0 (dated). The README's 100,000-element data table is mislabeled 'fluxsort' while its graph says quadsort, so per-distribution numbers for quadsort itself are unreliable. Quadsort is slower than std::stable_sort on bit-reversal input. It is C code, usable from C++ via its header.
