name: blitsort
workload: In-memory stable sort of 100,000-element 32/64/128-bit arrays across many distributions (random order, random % 100, ascending, descending, sawtooth, random tail/half, etc.), 100 samples, via the author's wolfsort benchmark harness; README explicitly states 'Stablesort is g++'s std:stable_sort function'
claimed_speedup: random order, 64-bit: std::stable_sort avg 0.006207s vs blitsort avg 0.002518s, ~2.5x faster (derived from page data); random order, 32-bit: 0.006025s vs 0.002341s, ~2.6x faster (derived); much larger gaps on structured distributions (e.g. descending order: 0.000921s vs 0.000055s, ~17x, derived)
compiler_and_flags: g++ -O3 -w -fpermissive bench.c, on WSL 2 gcc version 7.5.0 (Ubuntu 7.5.0-3ubuntu1~18.04)
tradeoffs: stable, in-place (uses rotations instead of an O(n) swap buffer), qsort()-compatible C interface rather than a template/iterator-based API; also benchmarked against gfx::cpp-TimSort in the same table, where blitsort is faster in most but not all distributions
caveats: No CPU model is stated (only WSL 2/gcc 7.5.0), and the run is inside WSL rather than bare metal, so it falls short of tier A. The benchmark uses an old libstdc++ (gcc 7.5) and may not match current blitsort or current libstdc++. The biggest speedups are on already-ordered or patterned data, which favors adaptive sorts. On the same table blitsort is not faster everywhere: on 128-bit random order the averages are 0.011047s (std::stable_sort) vs 0.011423s (blitsort), and blitsort is slower on 'ascending tiles' (0.000948 vs 0.001397) and 'bit reversal' (0.001355 vs 0.002160). The Unlicense is a public-domain dedication with no patent grant.
found_via: Blogs/talks: found via cross-links from scandum/crumsort's 'Big O' comparison table and the wolfsort shootout referenced there (seed query "sorting algorithm faster than std::sort talk benchmark"); opened via gh api repos/scandum/blitsort and its README

verification.tier_reason: README section 'Benchmark: blitsort vs std::stable_sort vs gfx::timsort' has a data table with all quoted averages (64-bit random 0.006207 vs 0.002518, 32-bit random 0.006025 vs 0.002341, descending 0.000921 vs 0.000055), states compiler and flags (WSL 2 gcc 7.5.0, g++ -O3 -w -fpermissive bench.c) and uses the public wolfsort harness, but no CPU model is given, so it is C, not A.
verification.notes: All claimed numbers match the README table rows exactly, and the metadata checks out (Unlicense, 715 stars, last commit 2024-07-27, not a fork or archived). I only expanded the caveats to cover the 128-bit parity and the distributions where blitsort loses.

corrected_fields.caveats: No CPU model is stated (only WSL/gcc version), and the run is inside WSL rather than bare metal, so this falls short of tier A methodology; numbers are from a 2024 README so may not reflect the current libstdc++ or current blitsort code; the largest speedups occur on already-ordered/patterned data rather than pure random data, which is a favorable case for adaptive sorts

name: crumsort

name: voracious_radix_sort
workload: In-memory sort of i64 (and other primitive-type) arrays at sizes from 100 to 1000+ elements across ~25 synthetic distributions (uniform, +-1e9 range, ascending/descending +variants, Zipf, normal, sqrt, pipe organ, etc.), 5 iterations, single- and multi-threaded, run on the maintainer's own machine and checked into the repo's results/ directory
claimed_speedup: i64 uniform, 1,000 elements: Rust std stable sort ~36us (36.80 ns/item) vs Voracious trait sort ~23us (23.57 ns/item), ~1.56x (derived from page data). At this size Voracious ties Rust sort_unstable (23.64 ns/item) because it falls back to pdqsort. The radix advantage shows at large sizes: at 1,000,000 elements single-thread Voracious takes 9311us vs Rust sort_unstable 37945us (~4.1x) and Rust stable sort 66765us (~7.2x); at 10,000,000 elements 117667us vs 535417us (~4.6x) and 757896us (~6.4x) (derived from page data). Page columns are mean time in us, standard deviation in ns and time per item in ns.
compiler_and_flags: README 'Version' section lists rustc 1.46.0 stable as last tested. The results file is output from a cargo test run; the repo's .env exports RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" and the Makefile test target uses cargo test --release, but the exact invocation for this run is not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 3950x 16c/32t (per repos/lakwet/voracious_sort/results/benchmark_1_2_0/computer_spec)
tradeoffs: out-of-place variants use up to 2x memory; only sorts primitive types and custom structs (no String/Tuple/Array support); radix sort is only worthwhile on larger arrays, falling back to native Rust sort for small inputs; best performance requires per-CPU tuning constants ('profiling'), and the shipped defaults are calibrated for the author's own Ryzen 3950x machine, so gains may not transfer to other CPUs
caveats: This compares against Rust's own slice::sort/sort_unstable (the pdqsort-era implementations), not C++ std::sort, so compared_against_cpp_std_directly=false. Rust replaced these with driftsort/ipnsort in 1.81, so the baseline is outdated. Build flags for the run are not stated, which caps it at tier C. Below a few hundred to thousand elements Voracious falls back to Rust's pdqsort, so small-array 'wins' are only against the stable sort; the real radix gains (4-7x vs Rust sorts) appear at 1M+ elements. The trait sort may use up to 2x memory (out of place).

name: vxsort-cpp
baseline: scalar introsort ported from the .NET CoreCLR GC (gcsort::introsort_orig), not std::sort
workload: Single-core sorting of 4,096 to 1,048,576 elements. For int64, vxsort (AVX2, unroll 1/4/8/12) is compared against a scalar introsort on 64-bit pointer arrays. The int32 tables cover vxsort only (unroll 1/4/8), with no baseline.
claimed_speedup: The README compares against 'Introspective Sort (Scalar Baseline)', which is a port of the .NET CoreCLR GC introsort sorting 64-bit pointers, not std::sort. It reports roughly 4.8x at 1M int64 with 8x unroll (55ns -> 11.5ns per element; the table gives 53.08ns vs 11.54ns, ~4.6x) and ~4.5x at 128K int64 (45ns -> 10.5ns). No std::sort numbers are published, and the int32 results have no baseline numbers.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler/version not stated (README recommends clang). CMakeLists defaults to a Release build. At the June 2020 commit behind the published results, Release flags for GCC/Clang were '-Ofast -DNDEBUG'; current master uses '-O2 -fomit-frame-pointer -DNDEBUG'.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X @ 3.8GHz
tradeoffs: Requires AVX2/AVX-512 x86 hardware; C++ port of the original C# VxSort library, described by its own author as an experimental/rough reimplementation; low adoption relative to other SIMD sorts in this list.
caveats: The published baseline is not std::sort. It is gcsort::introsort_orig, a scalar port of the .NET CoreCLR GC introsort, from the 2020 code (bench/BM_fullsort.int64_t.cpp at ec12899). Current master has bench/fullsort/BM_fullsort.stdsort.cpp, which calls std::sort, but no std::sort results are published. The README results date from 2020 and no longer match the current benchmark code. The compiler version is not stated. The Ryzen 3950X (Zen 2) has no AVX-512, so the published numbers are AVX2 only. The default branch was last committed on 2023-05-10. Recent activity (2026-06-12) is on an unrelated-history 'nextgen' branch.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "VxSort"

name: HighwayHash
workload: Hash inputs of 8, 31, 32, 63, 64, and 1024 bytes on a single idle core of a Xeon E5-2690 v3 (2.6GHz), comparing HighwayHashAVX2/SSE41 against SipHash, SipHash13, SipTreeHash and SipTreeHash13, measured in cycles/byte with a custom cycle-accurate nanobenchmark harness.
claimed_speedup: At 1024 bytes: HighwayHashAVX2 0.24 cycles/byte vs SipHash 1.26 cycles/byte -> ~5.25x faster (derived from page data, matching the README's own '5x faster' claim); at 64 bytes: HighwayHashAVX2 0.95 vs SipHash 1.93 -> ~2x faster (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Patched GCC 4.9, 64-bit, flags -std=c++11 -O3 -march=haswell -fno-exceptions -fno-tree-vrp -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fno-strict-aliasing -fPIE (flags stated in the linked arXiv paper 1612.06257, Sec. 5; README says only 'patched GCC 4.9')
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2690 v3, 2.6 GHz, single idle core
tradeoffs: SIMD-dependent (AVX2/SSE4.1/VSX), needs runtime CPU dispatch for portability; the hash output is explicitly declared 'frozen forever' so no further algorithmic improvements will ever land; repository is archived by Google (read-only) so no future compiler/security fixes.
caveats: Compared against SipHash/SipTreeHash, not std::hash. Benchmark used a patched, non-public GCC 4.9 build (the paper notes unmodified GCC 6.3 gives ~10% lower throughput and GCC 4.8.4 ~3x slower code) on ~2014-era Haswell-EP hardware, and the GitHub repository is archived (last commit 2024-04-18), so the numbers do not reflect modern compilers or CPUs. The accompanying arXiv paper is a preprint, not peer-reviewed.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "highwayhash"

verification.tier_reason: README 'Speed measurements' table shows HighwayHashAVX2 0.24 vs SipHash 1.26 cycles/byte at 1024 B and 0.95 vs 1.93 at 64 B, measured on a Xeon E5-2690 v3 with benchmark code in the repo (highwayhash/benchmark.cc + highwayhash/nanobenchmark.cc). The README omits flags, but the arXiv paper it links (1612.06257, Sec. 5) gives the compiler and exact flags, so all A criteria are met.
verification.notes: All README numbers match; the derived 5.25x (1 KiB) and ~2x (64 B) ratios are correct, and the paper itself says 5.2-5.3x vs SipHash at 1 KiB. Repo is archived with Apache-2.0 license and 1,603 stars; metadata is accurate.

name: komihash
workload: Hash short keys (0-15 bytes, 8-28 bytes) and 256,000-byte bulk buffers, averaged across 10 compiler/CPU combinations (GCC 11.5, Clang 18/19, ICC 19, clang-cl 18, Apple Clang 15) on Ryzen 3700X/9950X, Xeon E-2386G, Core i7-7700K, and Apple M1, measuring cycles/hash and GB/s.
claimed_speedup: Averages over all 10 compiler/CPU combos (overhead excluded): komihash 5.34 7.2 cycles/hash (0-15b) and 8.6 (8-28b) vs wyhash_final4 13.5/18.0, XXH3_64 14.2/21.8, XXH64 10.2/15.0. That works out to ~1.9-2.1x fewer cycles than wyhash_final4, ~2.0-2.5x fewer than XXH3_64 and ~1.4-1.7x fewer than XXH64 on short keys (derived from page data). On 256,000-byte bulk hashing komihash (19.3-42.7 GB/s) is slower than XXH3_64 (28.0-68.4 GB/s) on all 10 platforms and slower than wyhash_final4 on 8 of 10 (derived from page data), so the advantage is specific to short/medium keys.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.5.0 (-O3 -msse2 / -O3 -mavx2), LLVM Clang 19.1.7 (-O3 -mavx2), clang-cl 18.1.8 (/Ox -msse2 or -mavx2), ICC 19.0 (/O3 /QxSSE2), Apple Clang 15.0.0 (-O3) -- full 10-combo matrix given in the README
hardware: AMD Ryzen 3700X (4.2GHz) and Ryzen 9950X (5.7GHz), Intel Xeon E-2386G (5.1GHz), Core i7-7700K (4.5GHz), Apple M1 (3.5GHz)
tradeoffs: Non-cryptographic hash, not adversarial-collision-resistant without seeding; header-only C (compiles as C++) but exposes plain C functions (komihash(), komirand()) rather than a std::hash<T> specialization, so it needs a small wrapper to drop into unordered_map/unordered_set.
caveats: Never benchmarked against std::hash itself: the evidence is against best-in-class non-cryptographic hashes (xxHash, wyhash), not the std::hash baseline. The numbers are the author's own, and the benchmark exists only as an inline README snippet that relies on unpublished timer helpers (TClock/CSystem); the bulk GB/s test code is not published. On bulk throughput komihash loses to XXH3_64 on every listed platform.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "komihash"

verification.tier_reason: The README 'Comparisons' section gives the compiler, flags and CPU for all 10 platforms, plus the exact measurement loop (README inline code block using komihash/wyhash/XXH3_64bits calls), comparing against xxHash and wyhash. The timer helpers (TClock/CSystem) and the bulk-test code are not published, but the cycles/hash loop can be reproduced as given.
verification.notes: Every quoted number is on the README. I tightened the ratio range (vs XXH3_64 on 8-28b it is ~2.5x) and made the bulk caveat more precise (XXH3_64 wins bulk on all 10 platforms, not just 'some'). Metadata is accurate: MIT, 286 stars, last commit 2026-08-04, not archived.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Averaged over all 10 combos: komihash 5.34 needs ~7.2 cycles/hash (0-15b) and ~8.6 cycles/hash (8-28b) vs wyhash_final4's 13.5/18.0 and XXH3_64's 14.2/21.8 -- roughly 1.9-2x fewer cycles on short keys (derived from page data). On 256KB bulk hashing the result is mixed: komihash reaches up to 42.7 GB/s but XXH3_64 reaches up to 68.4 GB/s on some platforms, so komihash's advantage is specific to short/medium keys, not bulk throughput.

name: MUM/VMUM hash
baseline: xxHash3, Google CityHash (City64), Bob Jenkins SpookyHash, SipHash24, MetroHash, t1ha2 — widely-used non-cryptographic hash functions used in place of std::hash for hash-table keys
workload: Hashing 1,280M keys of lengths from 3 to 1024 bytes, plus 10,000 x 16MB bulk keys, on four different machines; each measurement repeated 3x and the minimum time kept.
claimed_speedup: Geomean of relative throughput across key lengths, VMUM-V2 normalized to 1.00 (higher/lower time = slower/faster): on Apple M4, VMUM-V2 is ~1.3x faster than xxHash3 (ratio 0.79), ~2.6x faster than CityHash (0.38), and ~4.8x faster than SipHash24 (0.21); on IBM Power10 it's roughly on par with xxHash3 (0.93) and ~2.1x faster than CityHash (0.48). (derived from page data: the README's per-length tables list ratio+time for VMUM-V1/V2, MUM-V3/V4, Spooky, City, xxHash3, t1ha2, SipHash24 and Metro on AMD Ryzen 9900X, an Intel chip, IBM Power10 and Apple M4.)
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2.1 (AMD Ryzen 9900X and Apple M4), GCC 12.3.1 (Intel), GCC 11.5.0 (IBM Power10); -O3 for all. benchmarks/bench.sh also appends -march=native on x86_64 and -mcpu=native on ppc64, and adds -flto only for the competing hash functions (not MUM/VMUM) to allow cross-file inlining. Each test is run 3x pinned with taskset -c 0 and the minimum user time is kept.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9900X, Intel i5-13600K (the README prose says 'i5-1300K'), Intel Core Ultra 9 285 (table only), IBM Power10, Apple M4 10-core Mac mini
tradeoffs: VMUM needs target SIMD (AVX2 on x86-64, NEON on aarch64, Altivec on ppc64) to get its full speed advantage on mid/long keys, falling back to scalar emulation elsewhere; an earlier VMUM/MUM-V3 had a collision-attack weakness (fixed Nov 2025 at ~10% extra cost, now default); requires compiler support for 128-bit integer extensions.
caveats: There is no LICENSE file and GitHub reports no SPDX license, but every source header (mum.h, vmum.h, mum512.h, mum-prng.h) carries the MIT permission notice. The benchmark is first-party (author's repo) but fully disclosed. xxHash3 is not beaten everywhere: it is faster than VMUM-V2 on mid-size keys (about 32/64-128 bytes, and 16 bytes on Power10; e.g. 128 bytes: 1.98x on AMD, 1.81x on M4, 2.03x on Power10) and on bulk on AMD/M4. VMUM-V1 is itself ~1.1x faster than VMUM-V2 on geomean. Timings are whole-program user time, including key generation.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): located via GitHub metadata lookup while following up leads from the SMHasher hash-function shootout referenced by rapidhash's README, in response to the seed query 'hash function benchmark std::hash comparison'.

verification.notes: The claimed ratios match the M4 and Power10 geomean rows. The license is MIT via per-file headers, not unlicensed, so usability changes from reference to copyable. The tables cover 5 machines, including an Intel Ultra 9 285 not mentioned in the prose. Metadata verified: 165 stars, last commit 2026-06-02, not a fork or archived.

name: sse4-strstr (SIMD-friendly algorithms for substring searching)
baseline: std::strstr / libc strstr (same problem as std::string::find and the default std::search)
workload: Scan a fixed text corpus (data/i386.txt) for a word list (data/words) with SWAR/SSE2/SSE4.1/SSE4.2/AVX2 substring-search kernels vs std::strstr, timed end-to-end, on an Intel Skylake i7-6700 with GCC 5.4.1.
claimed_speedup: std::strstr: 0.662s vs AVX2 (generic) kernel: 0.364s -> ~1.82x faster (derived from page data); SSE2 (generic): 0.489s -> ~1.35x faster (derived from page data). Other machines in the results folder (Haswell, Cascade Lake, Knights Landing, ARMv7/ARMv8) show similar or larger gaps.
compiler_and_flags: g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -I. -DHAVE_SSE_INSTRUCTIONS -mavx2 -DHAVE_AVX2_INSTRUCTIONS -DNDEBUG (current Makefile speedup_avx2 target). GCC 5.4.1 for the cited result (from the result filename). results/ also has GCC 4.8.4-7.4.0 and Clang 3.8.0 runs on other CPUs.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 (Skylake) for the cited number. results/ also covers ARMv7, ARMv8 (Clang 3.8.0), AMD Bulldozer FX-8510, Intel Haswell i7-4770, Knights Landing 7210, Skylake i9-7900, Cascade Lake Xeon Gold 5217, and Westmere M540.
tradeoffs: Companion code for a blog article (0x80.pl), not a packaged library -- integrating it means vendoring individual .cpp/.h kernels rather than linking a target; only exact single-needle substring search is covered (no wide-char, no custom predicates, no std::string_view-style API).
caveats: Companion sample code for a 2016-era article on SIMD substring search. Last commit January 2022 (abandoned). The ~1.8x figure is for one kernel/CPU pairing, and results vary widely by kernel and machine in results/. The 'std::strstr' row is the unqualified C strstr (glibc on the GCC/Linux runs), not the generic std::search. speedup.cpp deliberately skips std::string::find on GCC builds ('proven to be utterly slow'), so it has no numbers on x86.

name: StringZilla
workload: Find the first occurrence of a random ~5-byte word in text, measured as throughput (GB/s) on an Intel Xeon4 (Sapphire Rapids, GCC+glibc) and an Apple M5 Pro (Apple Clang+libc++).
claimed_speedup: Find first ~5-byte random word: STL std::string::find 9.1 GB/s vs StringZilla sz_find 21.0 GB/s on Xeon4 (~2.3x, derived from page data) and 10.9 vs 37.1 GB/s on M5 Pro (~3.4x, derived from page data); glibc strstr 21.3 GB/s on Xeon4 matches sz_find (3.5 GB/s on M5 Pro). Split lines on \n/\r: STL std::string::find_first_of 1.1 vs sz_find_byteset 13.8 GB/s on Xeon4 (~12.5x, derived from page data) and 4.1 vs 23.7 GB/s on M5 Pro (~5.8x, derived from page data); libc strcspn 9.2 / 3.8 GB/s (numbers verbatim from README Performance table)
compiler_and_flags: GCC with glibc on Xeon4; Apple clang with libc++ on M5 Pro. Compiler versions and optimization flags for the published numbers are not stated (CONTRIBUTING.md only gives generic CMake Release build instructions).
hardware: Intel Sapphire Rapids ('Xeon4', exact SKU not given); Apple M5 Pro (18-core)
tradeoffs: Header-only C core plus C++/Python/Rust/Go/Swift/JS/C#/Java bindings; adopting it means switching from std::string::find to sz::find/sz::string (a search-and-replace, per the README's own comparison table), not a drop-in override of std::string itself; portability across NEON/AVX2/AVX-512/SVE/RVV/WASM backends adds build-system complexity; its own hash function (AES-based) is a separate, non-standard hasher, not a std::hash specialization.
caveats: First-party numbers. The README says 'Treat these as a first impression, not a benchmark suite' and 'These will not reproduce exactly'. Compiler versions and flags are not stated. glibc strstr is on par with sz_find on Xeon4, so the big wins are over std::string::find and find_first_of and over the weaker Apple libc.

name: t1ha (Fast Positive Hash)
baseline: xxHash32 (also xxHash64 and the Murmur2/Murmur3 family) in SMHasher speed tests
workload: SMHasher speed tests from 2016 on an Intel Core i7-6700K (README 'Scores' tables): average cycles/hash over 1-31-byte keys and bulk MiB/s on a 262144-byte block, comparing t1ha / t1ha_aes against xxHash32/64, Murmur2/3, FNV1a, CRC32/64-HW, MUM, City/Farm/Metro/Spooky and others.
claimed_speedup: Small keys (1-31 bytes, avg cycles/hash): t1ha_aes 33.03 and t1ha 35.55 vs xxHash32 43.72, which is ~1.32x and ~1.23x fewer cycles (derived from page data). Large keys (262144-byte block, MiB/s): t1ha_aes 34,636.42 and t1ha 12,228.80 vs xxHash32 5,513.55, i.e. ~6.3x and ~2.2x (derived from page data), or ~3.1x and ~1.1x vs xxHash64's 11,123.15 MiB/s (derived from page data). The ~6.3x/~2.2x figures are bulk-throughput ratios, not small-key ones.
compiler_and_flags: gcc version 5.4.0 20160609 (Ubuntu 5.4.0-6ubuntu1~16.04.4), CFLAGS: -march=native -O3 -fPIC
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700K
tradeoffs: t1ha_aes variant is non-portable (requires AES-NI); several other variants (t1ha_32le/be) are explicitly flagged by the author as 'alien' -- designed for niche 32-bit or big-endian targets, not general-purpose use; t1ha0 dispatches to the fastest available implementation at runtime, adding a small indirection cost.
caveats: The benchmark data is from 2016 on a Skylake i7-6700K with GCC 5.4, and the exact SMHasher revision is not stated. The README's newer self-benchmark (make check, i7-4600U, GCC 9.3, flags unstated) shows t1ha2_atonce at 17.25 cycles/hash on 7-byte keys vs xxhash32 16.5, xxh3_64 15.1 and wyhash_v7 14.1, so t1ha2 is not faster on tiny keys against modern hashes; on 16 KiB keys t1ha2 (0.213 c/B) beats xxh3_64 (0.301) but roughly ties wyhash_v7 (0.206). The GitHub repo is an archived mirror: per the README, GitHub deleted the author's account in 2022, the repo was later restored read-only, and the origin moved to GitFlic. Compares against xxHash/Murmur, not std::hash.

name: rapidhash
baseline: xxh3 (xxHash3) — not literally std::hash, but the widely-used fast non-cryptographic hash function developers use in place of std::hash
workload: Average per-hash latency hashing 4/8/16-byte keys, and peak throughput hashing 16KB-2MB files, measured on several CPUs.
claimed_speedup: Latency on M1 Pro: 1.79ns vs xxh3's 1.92ns; on M3 Pro: 1.38ns vs 1.50ns; on Neoverse V2: 2.05ns vs 2.15ns; roughly on par on Ryzen 9700X (1.46ns vs 1.45ns). Peak throughput on M4: 71GB/s vs xxh3's 49GB/s (~45% faster, derived from page data); on M3 Ultra 61GB/s vs 47GB/s; on Neoverse V2 38GB/s vs 34GB/s; xxh3 is faster on Ryzen 9700X (78GB/s vs rapidhash's 68GB/s).
hardware: Apple M1 Pro, M3 Pro, M3 Ultra, M4; ARM Neoverse V2; AMD Turin; AMD Ryzen 9700X (per README tables; AMD Turin appears only in the latency table)
stars_or_usage: 907 stars; used in Chromium, Node.js, Folly's F14, Fuchsia, Ninja, JuliaLang, and Zig
tradeoffs: No cryptographic security guarantees; avoids CLMUL/AES-NI so it stays portable across x86-64 and aarch64; ships three variants (rapidhash/Micro/Nano) trading long-input throughput for small-input latency or code size.
caveats: The README performance tables name the CPUs tested but not the compiler version or flags; they note only that long-input measurements used the RAPIDHASH_UNROLLED macro. The bench/ harness (adapted from xxHash's benchHash, GPLv2-licensed Makefile) defaults to CFLAGS -O3, but nothing confirms that setting produced the published table. xxh3 wins peak throughput on Ryzen 9700X (78 vs 68 GB/s) and ties on latency there. Independent corroboration: rurban/smhasher's summary table (default AMD Ryzen 5 3350G) lists rapidhash at 21513.71 MiB/s and 22.04 cycles/hash vs xxh3 at 20853.74 MiB/s and 29.46 cycles/hash (compiler/flags not stated there either).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): rapidhash's own README states it is 'the fastest recommended hash function by SMHasher and SMHasher3', i.e. it is the harvested winner of the SMHasher/SMHasher3 hash-quality-and-speed shootouts, found while chasing the seed query 'hash function benchmark std::hash comparison'.

verification.tier_reason: The README tables (first-party, bench/ harness adapted from xxHash benchHash, compiler/flags unstated) alone would be C, but the independent rurban/smhasher suite, which the README links, also shows rapidhash ahead of xxh3 (21513.71 vs 20853.74 MiB/s bulk; 22.04 vs 29.46 cycles/hash small keys on its default AMD Ryzen 5 3350G), without stating compiler/flags, so B holds.
verification.notes: All README numbers match the record, including the ~45% M4 derivation (71 vs 49 GB/s). The record omitted AMD Turin (latency 2.31ns vs xxh3 2.35ns); I fixed hardware and added the SMHasher corroboration to caveats. Metadata checks out: MIT, 907 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-08-19.

name: Boost.Algorithm Boyer-Moore / Boyer-Moore-Horspool searchers
workload: Search a 2,756,252-entry random 8-bit corpus for a 105-entry pattern (middle), a 43-entry pattern (end) and a 91-entry pattern (not found), using boost::algorithm::boyer_moore_search / boyer_moore_horspool_search vs std::search, via Boost.Algorithm's test/search_test2.cpp.
claimed_speedup: std::search: 0.4848s (100%, baseline) vs boyer_moore_search: 0.1171s (24.16%) vs boyer_moore_horspool_search: 0.1076s (22.2%) for a 105-char pattern found mid-corpus -- i.e. boyer_moore ~4.1x faster, boyer_moore_horspool ~4.5x faster than std::search (derived from page data; percentages are verbatim from the PR). A second case (91-char 'not found' pattern) shows std::search 1.028s vs boyer_moore_horspool 0.1825s (~5.6x, derived from page data).
stars_or_usage: 131 stars; boyer_moore_search/boyer_moore_horspool_search ship in mainline Boost.Algorithm and are used wherever Boost is deployed
tradeoffs: Boyer-Moore/Horspool searchers build an O(alphabet + pattern) skip table before searching, which pays off when reused or on longer patterns but adds overhead for a single tiny one-off search; since C++17 the same two algorithms are also standardized as std::boyer_moore_searcher / std::boyer_moore_horspool_searcher, usable directly with std::search -- so on a C++17+ toolchain the standard library itself can close most of this gap without Boost.
caveats: The quoted numbers come from PR #25, opened in 2016 by contributor Jeremy Murphy (jeremy-murphy), not Marshall Clow. The PR proposes a Musser-Nishanov searcher and is still open and unmerged. The timing rows used here are for the already-mainline boyer_moore/boyer_moore_horspool searchers. Compiler, flags, CPU model and standard library are not stated, and the author warns of 5-10% run-to-run variance, so treat the ~4-5x figures as indicative. The baseline is plain std::search; since C++17 the standard also ships std::boyer_moore_searcher and std::boyer_moore_horspool_searcher (derived from these Boost searchers), which this PR does not compare against.
found_via: WebSearch: "faster than std::search" OR "beats std::search" C++ benchmark github -> github.com/boostorg/algorithm/pull/25

verification.tier_reason: PR #25 shows edited search_test2 output (the benchmark code test/search_test2.cpp is in the mainline repo) timing std::search against boyer_moore_search and boyer_moore_horspool_search. It gives no compiler, flags, CPU or standard library, so the tier is C.
verification.notes: The numbers match the PR exactly (4.1x/4.5x middle, 5.6x not-found). The caveat misattributed the PR to Marshall Clow; its author is jeremy-murphy. last_commit on the default branch (develop) is 2026-08-05; 2026-08-12 is the repo pushed_at, not a default-branch commit. BSL-1.0, 131 stars and active status are all accurate.

corrected_fields.caveats: The quoted numbers come from Marshall Clow's (Boost.Algorithm's maintainer) still-open, unmerged PR #25 (from 2016, proposing an additional Musser-Nishanov searcher); the timing table is for the already-mainline boyer_moore/boyer_moore_horspool searchers, not the unmerged musser_nishanov code. Compiler, flags, and CPU model are not stated in the PR, so treat the ~4-5x figures as indicative rather than reproducible as-is; the author notes run-to-run variance of 5-10%.
corrected_fields.workload: Locate an ~105 or ~43-character pattern (present in the middle/end, or absent) inside a 2,756,252-character random 8-bit text corpus, using boost::algorithm::boyer_moore_search / boyer_moore_horspool_search vs std::search, via the Boost.Algorithm search_test2 benchmark tool.

name: CityHash
baseline: MurmurHash2/MurmurHash3 (Murmur2, Murmur3F, Murmur3A) — widely-used non-cryptographic hash functions used in place of std::hash
workload: Hashing short strings (1, 8, 64 bytes) and long strings, on a single core of a 2.67GHz Intel Xeon X5550.
claimed_speedup: CityHash64 v1.0.3: 7ns for 1 byte vs Murmur2's 6ns (Murmur2 slightly faster here) but 9ns for 64 bytes vs Murmur2's 15ns and Murmur3F's 23ns (roughly 1.7x-2.5x faster at 64 bytes, derived from page data). CityHashCrc256 peaks at about 5-5.5 bytes/cycle on long strings vs the fastest Murmur variant (Murmur3F) at about 2.4 bytes/cycle (roughly 2x-2.3x faster, derived from page data).
hardware: Single core, 2.67GHz Intel Xeon X5550
stars_or_usage: 1.2k stars; historically used in many hash-table/database implementations before Google's own successors (FarmHash, Abseil's hash) superseded it
tradeoffs: No incremental/streaming API; not SIMD/AVX-optimized the way modern hashes (xxh3, rapidhash) are; the CRC-based variants depend on the _mm_crc32_u64 intrinsic being available.
caveats: Repository is archived by Google and had its last real commit in 2022; the README's benchmark numbers date to roughly the CityHash v1.0.3/1.1 era (~2011) on now-obsolete server hardware, do not state compiler flags, and are not compared against any modern hash (xxh3, rapidhash, wyhash); tier capped at C because compiler/flags are unstated for these specific numbers.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): surfaced while cataloguing hash-function shootout history referenced from rurban/smhasher and rapidhash's README, in response to the seed query 'hash function benchmark std::hash comparison'.

verification.tier_reason: First-party README numbers against Murmur2/Murmur3F on a single core of a 2.67GHz Xeon X5550, with no stated compiler/flags and no benchmark harness in the repo (src/ has only city.cc, city.h, citycrc.h, city-test.cc).
verification.notes: The README matches the record verbatim: 7/6/9ns vs Murmur2 6/6/15ns and Murmur3F 14/15/23ns; CityHashCrc256 at 5-5.5 bytes/cycle vs Murmur3F at 2.4 bytes/cycle. The derived ratios (about 1.7x-2.6x at 64 bytes, 2.1x-2.3x on long strings) hold. gh api shows the repo is archived, MIT, 1231 stars, not a fork, last commit 2022-07-19, so 'abandoned' is correct.
